articles.title: Microsoft’s Brad Smith pushes back on Vice President JD Vance’s visa fraud accusations
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft President Brad Smith says someone apparently “failed to inform the vice president accurately about our numbers” before the Trump administration cut off the company’s ability to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency.

In an interview with Politico , published Thursday, Smith rejected Vice President JD Vance’s accusations of fraud and called his claim that Microsoft replaced laid-off Americans with foreign workers “completely off base.” He said Microsoft has “always been committed to a high integrity and high compliance” approach to immigration.
“We will stand by our record,” Smith said. “And I hope that folks at the White House might look again and look at what we think is a more accurate picture.”
At a White House news conference last week, Vance said Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers last year while receiving 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.

“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said, after asserting that there “has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft.”

Critics of the visa programs say tech companies have used them to displace U.S. workers, and that the job ads companies must run before sponsoring workers for green cards often appear in places few American job seekers will see. Labor Department records show Microsoft’s required print ads ran mostly in The Seattle Times.

Smith said most of Microsoft’s recent visa and green card applications were for people already working at the company, many of them for years, because of long green card backlogs. He also said Microsoft hired 9,200 American workers in its last fiscal year, a number he said was “left out of the narrative.”

The Microsoft executive also rejected the idea that the company pays visa holders less. “It doesn’t matter whether you came on a visa or you’re an American worker,” he said. “Everybody has the same compensation system.”

He warned that the crackdown could send “the most talented next wave” of engineers to other countries. Five of the six tech leaders President Trump honored with national medals last week, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella , came to the U.S. as immigrants, Smith noted, and their companies together account for more than 25% of the value of the S&P 500.
The suspension doesn’t stop Microsoft from hiring foreign workers on H-1B visas. Those are temporary work visas, typically granted for three years at a time and generally limited to six.

Amazon led in H-1B approvals for new employment in fiscal 2025, with 4,644, followed by Meta with 1,555 and Microsoft with 1,394, according to an analysis of USCIS data by the National Foundation for American Policy.

What Microsoft lost is access to a key step toward permanent residency. The program, known as PERM , is run by the Labor Department. Companies use it to sponsor foreign employees for permanent residency, also known as a green card. The employer has to advertise the job and show the department that no qualified, available U.S. worker can fill it.
PERM is commonly used for employees already working in the U.S. on temporary visas, including H-1Bs.

The interview didn’t address Microsoft’s outsized use of PERM. The company had more PERM cases decided than any other employer in fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026, according to a GeekWire analysis of Labor Department data. Other big tech companies, including Amazon and Google, sharply reduced their PERM filings after early 2023.

articles.title: Startup Spotlight: Zeacon aims to turn website visitors into buyers with AI-powered video
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Businesses spend heavily to attract visitors to their websites, but traffic doesn’t necessarily translate into sales. Bellevue, Wash.-based Zeacon is building AI tools to help companies connect their marketing content with customer behavior and understand what actually drives conversions.

Co-founded by Kris Naidu and Jay Gounder , Zeacon uses AI to generate videos, personalize website content and track how visitors interact with it. The platform is also designed to identify bot traffic and analyze how both people and AI agents navigate websites — an increasingly important capability as AI changes how people discover and interact with businesses online.

Zeacon’s goal is to help companies move beyond traffic and content creation to understand what turns visitors into customers. As Naidu and Gounder see it, the real measure of success isn’t how many visitors a website attracts, but how many convert.
We caught up with Kris Naidu for our latest Startup Spotlight.
In 50 words or less, give us your elevator pitch :

We help businesses deploy AI agents that optimize their entire digital funnel, with an initial focus on video. Our AI agents can autonomously generate video content without prompting, publish it across social media and websites, personalize the experience for each website visitor and identify bots, while continuously analyze and optimize performance.
What problem are you obsessed with solving?

We are obsessed with helping businesses turn the attention they already paid for into sales. Brands invest in advertising and great video content, but the website where customers actually buy often doesn’t connect with those investments. Zeacon brings that content onto the website, personalizes it to the visitor, and connects engagement to buying behavior. We can also create new videos from product photos and website data based on what converts. The question driving us is simple: How can we help this business sell more while taking work off its team?
What surprised you after talking to customers?

How much opportunity exists in what they already have. Businesses have videos, product photos, website traffic, and customer data. What’s missing is the connection between them. A marketing team wants to know: Which content helps people buy? Where are we losing customers? What should we create next? That reinforced our belief that the real value is turning information into a decision they can act on which we can provide with our platform.
How has artificial intelligence changed the way you build your company?

AI changed what we could take off the customer’s plate. Zeacon can understand website and product information, generate video from pictures without prompting, choose relevant content for a visitor, and help teams ask questions about performance in plain English. We’re building those capabilities together: create, personalize, measure, and learn. Each result can inform the next decision. That’s a much bigger opportunity than making content faster which we can also do but it means helping a business continuously improve how it sells.
What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That revenue alone does not tell you how valuable an AI company is. Revenue matters it proves customers will pay. But data deserves equal attention because it determines what the system can learn and how useful it becomes. At Zeacon, we care about the connection between visitor behavior, content, and conversion. The advantage comes from the quality of that data and our ability to turn it into better customer outcomes. Investors should ask what a company is learning with every deployment, alongside what it earns that will help them understand the true growth value. Upfront value without long term vision effects companies and we were always focused on the end goal which was delivering a product that adds value not only in the near term but cannot be easily replaced.
What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Deciding what to say no to. When your technology opens up several opportunities, it’s tempting to pursue all of them. But customers need you to solve their problem well. Our focus is helping businesses use video and data to improve their website experience and grow sales. We have to judge opportunities against that purpose, even when they’re exciting. The data helped us understand the entire flow of users for our customers that when we had our moment. We realized it just was not about providing outcomes for sales but helping the customers fix issues within their website journey and using the content to help fill gaps for the desired outcomes.
What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Focus. Get close to your customers, understand the problem they will pay you to solve, and keep delivering against it. Do not confuse more features with more value. Make something customers use, trust, and want to keep. It is hard but being focused is the key to winning.
Zeacon is recognized for creating a new business science on relating content and user behavior to actual business outcomes.

articles.title: Lime tops 10.5M Seattle rides in 2026, rolling past last year’s e-bike and scooter total two months early
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Lime riders in Seattle have already outpaced last year’s entire ridership numbers, logging more than 10.5 million trips through October — surpassing the city’s 2025 full-year total a full two months ahead of schedule.

Powered by a massive surge during the summer’s FIFA World Cup matches in Seattle and a record-breaking Seahawks Super Bowl parade, the milestone highlights how deeply e-bikes and scooters have embedded themselves into Seattle’s daily commute and transit network.

The summer soccer tournament alone accounted for more than 1.7 million trips, headlined by an all-time single-day high of 83,000 rides on June 19 for the USA vs. Australia match — a record notably boosted by Seahawks legend Marshawn Lynch joining the “march to the match.”

That single-day mark shattered the previous high-water mark of nearly 60,000 rides set during the Seahawks parade in February. Four of Lime’s top five all-time ridership days in Seattle occurred during the World Cup stretch.

“We’re extremely proud of our partners at SDOT, who have spent years building a program and infrastructure that compelled our CEO to call Seattle ‘the next micromobility-first city,'” Lime’s Hayden Harvey, a regional director of government relations, said in a statement. “We’re also grateful to our riders, the Seattleites who choose day in and day out; rain or shine, two wheeled transportation instead of four.”

The record-setting volume reflects Lime’s position as the only game in town. After rival operators exited the market, Lime became the exclusive vendor in the City of Seattle’s micromobility share program .
Lime has since scaled its footprint to 15,000 active devices that are serviced and staged out of a sprawling warehouse south of downtown in Georgetown.

Beyond fleet expansion, Lime is leaning into affordability to convert event riders into daily commuters. Alongside its existing LimeAccess program for low-income riders and its $5.99 monthly LimePrime subscription — which now counts more than 38,000 monthly subscribers in Seattle — the company rolled out a new commuter-hours pricing pilot this week that lowers per-minute rates during daytime travel windows.

articles.title: Seattle-area innovators shine on Time’s ‘Best Inventions’ list, from tactile tablets to ultrasonic knives
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Seattle-area innovators made a strong showing on Time’s 2026 Best Inventions list released Thursday, claiming spots for breakthroughs ranging from a tactile sports tablet for low-vision fans to an ultrasonic chef’s knife.

The annual roundup — featuring 300 innovations, with Apple CEO John Ternus and the new iPhone Duo gracing the cover — includes startups like Yoodli, Tin Can, and OneCourt, alongside major regional hardware operations like SpaceX’s Redmond-based Starlink team and Bellevue’s Valve.

While the main headline focused on Apple’s leadership transition and new flagship hardware, the Pacific Northwest’s outsized presence on this year’s list highlights the region’s growing influence across everything from consumer AI and assistive hardware to outdoor gear.

Among the region’s tech giants, Amazon landed two spots on the list, for both its Amazon Pharmacy Kiosk in the medical category and its voice-directed Proteus warehouse robots in logistics. But Microsoft was shut out entirely, missing a placement in both the main 300 list and special mentions.

“These are creations changing how we live, work, play, and think about what’s possible,” Time’s editor’s wrote, adding that each contender was evaluated on key factors, including originality, efficacy, ambition, and impact.
Here’s a breakdown of regional innovations honored by Time:

OneCourt (Accessibility): Developed a tactile tablet that translates real-time player and ball data into physical vibrations, allowing blind and low-vision fans to track live sports action with their fingertips.
Yoodli (Education): Recognized for its AI platform for human skills, which uses realistic AI roleplays and real-time coaching to help users build and practice workplace communication skills.
Tin Can (Parenting): Earned a spot for its landline-style home phone built specifically for kids, offering a safe way for families to stay connected without screens.

Seattle Ultrasonics C-200 (Food & Drink): Created by Modernist Cuisine alum Scott Heimendinger, this ultrasonic chef’s knife vibrates tens of thousands of times per second to slice effortlessly through food.

SpaceX Starlink V5 (Connectivity): Engineered by SpaceX’s team in Redmond, the newest internet terminal is roughly 35% smaller and 52% lighter than its predecessor, making on-the-go satellite connectivity easier to mount and deploy.
Valve Steam Machine (Entertainment & Gaming): The Bellevue-based gaming giant made the list for its latest hardware push to bring PC gaming into the living room.
NBBJ (Architecture): The legendary Seattle-founded architecture firm was recognized for its design of the Life and Mind Building at the University of Oxford.
Pebblebee Halo (Privacy & Security): Created by the Issaquah-based startup founded by former Boeing engineers, earning a special mention for its latest tracking and safety hardware.
Therm-a-Rest NeoLoft (Outdoors): Honored for its ultra-comfortable sleeping pad, designed under Seattle-based parent company Cascade Designs.
Superfeet ME3D (Sports & Fitness): Selected for its personalized 3D-printed insoles, crafted by the Ferndale, Wash.-based footwear innovation company.

Several other Pacific Northwest companies made the cut. Three Vancouver, B.C., startups earned recognition: Moment Energy for its clean energy storage made from second-life EV batteries, Glüxkind for its AI-powered self-pushing stroller, the Rosa, and Form for its Smart Swim 2 Pro real-time coaching goggles. And in Oregon, Nike secured a spot in apparel for its innovative ACG cooling running shirt.
The Oct. 26 issue of Time goes on sale on Friday.

articles.title: Space propulsion startup Agile Space opens Seattle-area engineering office to tap regional talent
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Space propulsion company Agile Space Industries is expanding its footprint to the Pacific Northwest, signing a sublease for a new engineering office in Bellevue, Wash.

Situated in the Sunset North office complex along Interstate 90, the nearly 5,740-square-foot space will initially house a half-dozen existing employees while scaling up to accommodate an engineering team of 20 to 30 people.

The effort is being led by Chief Technology Officer Jake Mills , a former propulsion engineer and crew member at Jeff Bezos’ Kent-based Blue Origin space venture. Mills joined Durango, Colo.-based Agile in June and the Bellevue hub will try to tap into more of the Seattle region’s deep aerospace talent pool for systems, design, and propulsion engineering.

Started in 2009 as Advanced Mobile Propulsion Technologies, Agile specializes in in-space chemical propulsion systems for satellites, lunar landers, and national security missions. Unlike booster rockets that launch payloads off the planet, the company’s hardware — including thrusters, propellant tanks, and integrated propulsion systems — takes over once spacecraft reach orbit, navigating everything from commercial constellations to lunar exploration.

“The talent pool there, manufacturing capabilities there, customer base there, supply chain based in Seattle, all make it very attractive to go there, and that is the reason we’re opening up the engineering office,” Mills told GeekWire.

Agile joins a bustling Pacific Northwest aerospace cluster anchored by heavyweights like Blue Origin, SpaceX’s Starlink engineering operations in Redmond, and a growing wave of startups and orbital logistics companies like Starfish Space.

Overall, Agile employs 178 people across the business. The majority of its workforce is based at its Durango headquarters, alongside an additive manufacturing center in Pennsylvania and a 25,000-square-foot test center breaking ground in Tulsa, Okla.
The Bellevue office is located at 3120-3180 139th Ave SE.

Backed by a $17 million Series A funding round earlier this year, Agile has scaled rapidly, and revenue over the last three years has more than tripled. Investors include Caruso Ventures, Howdy Partners, Lockheed Martin Ventures, Veteran Ventures, Denver Ventures, and Cortado Ventures, among others.

Even as Agile plants a flag in the region, the expansion comes amid growing caution over Washington state’s business climate. Mills noted that the company shares the same concerns recently voiced by Stoke Space CEO Andy Lapsa — who warned during Seattle Space Week in September that if starting over today, “I’m not sure we’d make the same decision” to build in Washington, given local tax and political pressures.

While Agile is eager to tap into the local engineering talent for its Bellevue office, Mills cautioned that future investments, such as a prospective manufacturing and system integration facility, could face headwinds if Washington doesn’t match the aggressive incentives and welcoming posture shown by competing states like Oklahoma.

“I’m just biased towards the opportunity that when you get all the right people in the right place and you have that competition, you have all the capabilities that you need in one place, great things happen,” Mills said. “As people disperse from that, you start to lose that opportunity.”

articles.title: Amazon’s new AI devices can listen to conversations and suggest things to buy — if you opt in
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Bee , the AI wearables startup Amazon acquired last year , makes devices that remember what people say in everyday conversations. A new update, announced Thursday morning, includes a feature that turns those passing remarks into shopping suggestions on Amazon.com.

For example, as described by Amazon , someone might mention offhand that they’re out of dish soap, and a product recommendation would show up on Amazon.com and in the Bee mobile and desktop apps. Amazon pitches it as a way for people to remember to buy things they need.

It’s the kind of thing many people have long suspected their phones of doing secretly, listening to conversations and serving up related content or ads. Researchers haven’t found evidence of that. Either way, Amazon’s twist is to do it openly — and to make it voluntary.
The feature is opt-in, meaning it won’t happen unless users choose to connect their Bee accounts to Amazon.com, and Bee says it won’t share data with Amazon without user consent.
The Amazon.com integration requires Bee Pro, a $12 monthly subscription that also includes unlimited conversation summaries and the ability to ask Alexa+ about things Bee has captured.

New hardware: The feature is part of a broader announcement that includes the first new Bee devices under Amazon’s ownership: Bee Frontier, a $74.99 wristband that can also clip onto clothing, and Bee Eclipse, which attaches magnetically to the back of a phone and starts at $99.99.

Bee Frontier, available now, has dual microphones, up to seven days of battery life and IP67 water resistance. Bee Eclipse, about the size of a credit card, runs more than 21 days on a charge and will be available soon, Amazon says.

Amazon says Bee lets people pay attention to a conversation instead of taking notes, keeping track of details such as when and where they agreed to meet a friend. The devices turn conversations into summaries, to-dos and reminders.

Users can read their summaries in the Bee mobile app or a new desktop app, formatted for different kinds of conversations, such as lectures, care plans and brainstorming sessions. Bee also picks up on recurring themes in conversations and suggests goals and actions.

Bee connects to apps including Gmail, Google Calendar and Microsoft Outlook. After a call or meeting, it can list action items, draft follow-up emails or create calendar invites based on the conversation.
Users can also link Bee to Apple HealthKit and to their photos. Most of those features, including the desktop app and third-party integrations, also require Bee Pro.
Without a subscription, Bee users get conversation summaries and 14 days of memory. New customers get 30 days of Bee Pro free.

How Bee handles privacy: Amazon says Bee runs on a system it calls Bee Private Compute, which processes conversations in an isolated environment where “no one, including Amazon, can access your data.” Audio is deleted after it’s processed, and transcripts are encrypted with keys controlled by the user’s device.

Both new devices turn on and off with a single button and show a light when they’re running. For phone calls, Bee Eclipse prompts users to get permission from the other people on the call each time it starts, according to Amazon.

Bee and Amazon: Amazon acquired Bee in July 2025 for an undisclosed price. At the time, the San Francisco startup, led by co-founders Maria de Lourdes Zollo and Ethan Sutin, had raised $7 million and sold a $49.99 wristband called Bee Pioneer.

Thursday’s update connects Bee to two of Amazon’s biggest consumer businesses: its online store, through the product recommendations; and Alexa+, the new version of its longtime voice assistant , by letting users ask Alexa+ on an Echo device about things Bee has captured.
Amazon isn’t the only tech giant betting on AI devices.

Bee also competes with startups such as Plaud, Omi and Friend, which make AI recorders and pendants that listen to conversations, and with AI notetaking apps such as Granola and Otter that work on a phone, with no extra device required.

On another front, Amazon is fighting to keep other companies’ AI agents out of its store. Last month it blocked Meta’s Muse assistant from shopping on Amazon.com, after earlier moves against shopping agents from Perplexity, Google and OpenAI.

articles.title: Despite Pushback, Updated RapidRide R Plans Include Scant Changes
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Updated plans for the future RapidRide R bus line between Downtown Seattle and Rainier Beach released this week include only a few changes to previous iterations of the project, with significant stop consolidation still planned along much of the eight-mile route despite community concerns.

The next RapidRide line to enter planning in Seattle, the R Line is set to replace the Route 7 along Rainier Avenue S by 2032, bringing upgrades to the Metro's second busiest bus line. Compared to an initial proposal put forward this summer , two stop pairs have been added for both northbound and southbound riders, including retained stops at Rainier Avenue S and S Walker Street and a new set of stops at Rainier Avenue S and S Grand Street. That change will help riders between Sound Transit's light rail stations at Judkins Park and Mount Baker more easily access bus stops, but riders further north or south could see longer walks to catch a frequent bus that is currently within easy reach.

If this plan is approved by the King County Council next month, the R Line will move forward with some major stops currently used by Route 7 riders not on the list, including 12th Ave S and Boren Ave S, Rainier Ave S and S Charles Street, and Rainier Ave S and S Andover Street. But the two stops between Judkins Park and Mount Baker do represent a response to community concerns about losing transit access along that specific stretch.

"The alignment proposal adds station pairs at Rainier Ave S & S Grand St and at Rainier Ave S & S Bayview St in response to updated ridership, new housing, community destinations, and public feedback, and retains the station pair at Rainier Ave S & S Walker St to serve nearby schools, the Lighthouse for the Blind, and riders affected by steep grades and difficult crossings," Metro's updated engagement summary notes. "Additionally, as design progresses, exact station locations will be determined by multiple conditions, including ongoing analysis and engagement."

The R Line has emerged as a major priority for King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, a bus line that connects neighborhoods across the council district he represented from 2020 to 2024. Before Zahilay took office, the R Line's budget was slashed by 25% in response to budget pressures at Metro, with a new total budget of $91.2 million.

Unlike most recent RapidRide lines including the under-construction I and J and Lines, King County does not plan to pursue federal matching funds , a fact that speaks to the current transit funding environment in D.C. But not being tethered to a USDOT grant agreement could potentially allow the County to move more quickly toward construction or implement upgrades in stages.

In releasing his biggest budget update since taking office last month, Zahilay proposed to advance $64.4 million in RapidRide R funding to the current two-year budget, in a move his office framed as intended to "build a strong partnership" with the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), also planning roadway improvements along Rainier Avenue S that are set to be implemented in the early 2030s.

""Our South Seattle communities deserve fast, reliable transit service. Residents have been waiting over a decade for the RapidRide R Line, and we are moving with urgency to deliver on this generational investment that will greatly enhance mobility while also making critical safety upgrades,” Zahilay said in an announcement of the updated plan Thursday. “During Metro’s community engagement over the summer, we heard directly from seniors, people with disabilities, and families who were concerned about losing stops along Route 7. In response to that feedback, the alignment plan proposes two additional stops. We know this will be a change for neighbors who have relied on Route 7 for years, and we will continue listening to community and working to ensure the R line meets the diverse needs of residents and riders in the Southend.”

With fewer stops to make, the R Line will move more quickly along its route, on top of planned transit speed and reliability investments including transit signal priority (TSP) and additional bus-only lanes on top of the stretches already in place. But expected time savings data for a trip on the future R Line still has not been released by Metro, a key ask of transit advocates trying to weigh the trade-offs that come with stop consolidation.

Long stretches of bus lanes that had been envisioned when the R Line entered planning nearly a decade ago are now fully implemented , including a long stretch of northbound Rainier Avenue between S Edmunds Street in Columbia City and S Grand Street just south of I-90. But Metro and SDOT have not announced any plans for transit priority along S Jackson Street, one of the current Route 7's biggest pain points.

"The Rainier Valley stop consolidation decision-making was done with data that is now fairly out of date," a September 15 letter from the advocacy group Rainier Valley Safe Streets stated. "New studies that take into account current and future ridership enabled by the large apartment complexes that have been completed since the previous studies should be done. We recognize that stop consolidation is a difficult thing to get right, but densification of the Rainier Valley, especially near Judkins Park might justify decreased stop spacing."

Metro leaders – and County Councilmembers – are likely to face a push to consider restoring even more stop pairs along the corridor, given gaps of up to a half-mile that would be created. Even in an official letter of support included in the proposal transmitted to the King County Council, Seattle's Transit Riders Union (TRU) voiced concerns that the two new stop pairs weren't enough to mitigate impacts.

"We appreciate that Metro took community feedback into account and added back additional stops between Judkins Station and Mt Baker," the letter from TRU's bus and transit subcommittee noted. "We are still concerned by the large gaps created by consolidation which effectively choose to convert this route from its current attempt to be both a local and long distance service into an express bus skipping past parts of the south end. We would like to see this project go to further planning with wiggle room on which stops to move and remove."

It also remains to be seen how Metro will address riders south of S Henderson Street in Rainier Beach, along the so-called "Prentice Loop" only served by select Route 7 trips now. That area is currently served by Metro Flex microtransit service, an option that fills in the gaps in Metro's network but is absolutely not a replacement for fixed-route transit.

"Community members emphasized that the Prentice Loop and related neighborhood connections in the Rainier View and lower Rainier neighborhoods are essential for reaching schools, grocery stores, clinics, youth programs, religious centers, parks, and everyday destinations not located directly on Rainier Avenue S," the engagement summary stated. "Riders shared that existing local service helps seniors, riders with disabilities, youth, caregivers, and families access places that would otherwise require long and steep walks."
Thursday's announcement included some additional details about the future of transit service throughout broader Rainier Beach.

"Metro is also evaluating how to maintain strong and convenient transit connections for people traveling to and from areas south of South Henderson Street that will not be directly served by RapidRide R Line," the statement read, referencing potential changes to the Route 106, 107, and the 9. "Before the RapidRide R Line launches, Metro will engage communities south of South Henderson Street to better understand local travel needs, priorities, and important destinations and connections."

Even though a vote to sign off on the planned stop locations is planned for next month, the County Council will not actually be required to sign off on any adjustments to the R Line's stops, with the proposed ordinance only set to require notification.

"Before the implementation of RapidRide R Line service, the executive shall notify the King County council and the city of Seattle of any substantial changes to station locations," the draft ordinance states. "Following the implementation of RapidRide R Line service, the Metro transit department shall consult with the city of Seattle before making any changes to the routing or station locations."
After that vote, the R Line will advance into the next stage of planning, where Metro will align route upgrades with the project's reduced budget.

"Specific scope changes haven’t been finalized yet," Metro spokesperson Al Sanders told The Urbanist last month . "Those decisions will come in the next phase of design, after we confirm the route and stop locations. Once that foundation is set, we’ll be able to evaluate which capital improvements provide the greatest benefit within the appropriated budget and make informed decisions about what to carry forward into design."

articles.title: 'Unfathomable Disaster' Looms Following Public Defender Pay Dispute
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: After being unable to reach a contract agreement with the Washington State Department of Public Defense (OPD), the venerable Washington Appellate Project (WAP) may have to close its doors at the end of the year. Should this happen, the state’s court system could be disrupted due to the loss of experienced attorneys, a backlog of cases, and a more discouraging landscape for new lawyers who are considering pursuing appellate public defense.

Founded in 1993, WAP is the state’s only non-profit appellate public defense law firm and has historically handled about 40% of public defense appeals in the state: that is, appeals brought by clients who can’t afford to pay their own attorneys.

WAP attorneys have argued many life-altering cases over the years, including State v. Blake in 2021, in which the Washington state Supreme Court found the law criminalizing drug possession to be unconstitutional, and State v. Gregory in 2018, in which the Court found the death penalty in the state to be unconstitutional because it was being applied in an arbitrary and racially biased manner. They also argued a case that became part of the Miller fix that reformed how people who committed crimes as juveniles are sentenced and given a chance at parole.
Those cases illustrate how appellate public defense has the ability to impact a large number of Washingtonians by winning a single case.

“When you make the systemic changes, and I think Blake is a great example of this, it didn't just affect our client, Miss Blake,” Greg Link, the executive director of WAP, told The Urbanist . “It affected literally hundreds of thousands of people who would never be our client or never could have been our client.”
However, WAP’s contract with the state expired at the end of June, and OPD and WAP have been unable to agree on a new contract, a dispute that has ultimately led to a lawsuit.
WAP has said that the contract offered to them began a new pay model that was both unethical and unsustainable for the firm.

“OPD is currently paying WAP at rates that are unsustainable for the organization and incompatible with the amount of work required to provide effective, ethical, quality representation,” WAP wrote in their filing. “OPD also refuses to negotiate with WAP in good faith regarding appropriate compensation and case weighting designations going forward. Instead, OPD is insisting on WAP's acceptance of contractual terms that would cause WAP's attorneys to violate their constitutional and professional obligations to clients. This includes a case weighting model that provides far less time per case than a recent OPD-funded workload study deemed necessary for effective, ethical, quality appellate representation.”

OPD, on the other hand, says they are meeting the new caseload standards for public defense issued by the state Supreme Court and that the other law firms with whom they contract are able to make the new contracts work.

“First of all, we have always tied our contracts between compensation and number of cases. That has always been the case in the past, and that is the case in the current situation as well,” Katrin Johnson, the deputy director for operations at OPD, told The Urbanist . “What did change is simply that we added language to ensure greater accountability.”
The new language allows OPD greater flexibility in reassigning a case to a different firm if the original firm is unable to begin work on it.
“What's new was that language about making adjustments, if mid-year, it's clear that the contractor lacks capacity,” Johnson explained.
Link said that where WAP disagrees isn’t with the number of cases being handled by one attorney, but rather about how each case is weighted, which determines how many hours can be used on that case.

The calculation for determining case weight has changed in the most recent OPD contracts. In the past, case weight was determined by counting trial transcript pages, with one credit equaling 800 pages. With the new caseload standards, case weight is factored by counting both transcript pages and clerks’ pages, but a credit now equals 1,000 pages.
However, the disagreement over case weight calculations appears to be more fundamental than this change.
“There’s no way to tell if a case will be straightforward or all-consuming,” said Austin Field, the elections chair for the public defense chapter of SEIU 925.
The OPD contract does contain provisions offering extraordinary compensation for case outliers that require more work, for which attorneys have to apply on a case-by-case basis.

Some more complicated appellate cases can only be handled by attorneys with more experience. Link said OPD hadn’t been regulating the type of cases it was sending to WAP in this regard, creating capacity issues for the firm.
“The issue boils down to this: the Washington Appellate Project wanted a contract where they would be paid at the full time amount, yet only do half of the number of cases,” Johnson said.
Link emphasized that the structure of the new contracts is inherently creating ethical conundrums for attorneys.

“The dispute is about more than just the numbers in a contract,” Link said. “The dispute is about how public defense for people on appeal is going to be delivered. It’s about some of the terms in the contract that create [...] an incentive for attorneys to really minimize the work on any given case in order to make the maximum amount of money, the sort of things that we really don't want in public defense.”
Six law professors in the state who teach legal ethics wrote a letter supporting WAP. The Washington Defender Association also support WAP’s position .

According to Johnson, WAP filed their lawsuit against OPD while the two parties were in the middle of negotiating a six-month interim contract. More recently, WAP and OPD failed to reach a resolution through mediation, and in early September, certain claims of the lawsuit were dismissed while others continue to be in play.
The remaining lawsuit centers on WAP seeking adequate funding for their continued representation of what they say is nearly 500 people.

Without receiving more funding for its work, WAP will have to close its doors by the end of the year, meaning its remaining clients will be left without attorneys mid-case. While Washington’s public defense system is already considered to be in crisis , an additional backlog created by WAP’s current cases could worsen an already difficult situation.

“OPD has no demonstrated capacity to assign new attorneys to these individuals any time soon,” Link said. “So the crisis that looms is that come January hundreds of people will be without the attorney they are constitutionally entitled to.”
When a new attorney comes onto a case, it generally adds several months to its timeline, according to Field.
In contrast, Johnson said that recruitment for public defense appellate attorneys has been going well.

“Because the Supreme Court had lowered those caseload standards, we had to do strong recruiting of additional contract attorneys for appellate work because mathematically, if the number of cases per attorney is lower, then you need more attorneys to handle the workload,” Johnson said. “And so, in the springtime, while we were having challenges with Washington Appellate Project, we were also, meanwhile, recruiting for additional attorneys because of the reduced caseload standard. What we found was many public defenders who were at that time in trial level practice who wanted to branch into and begin doing appellate work, and the number of talented attorneys wanting to join our program was surprisingly bigger than we expected.”

While OPD is providing free training on appellate practice as well as a resource attorney to meet regularly with new appellate attorneys, the decades of appellate experience housed within WAP won’t be easy to replace, especially since only more experienced attorneys are allowed to handle more serious cases.
Field told The Urbanist that if WAP closes its doors, it would be an “unfathomable disaster.”
“It’s impossible to overstate the importance of appellate public defense,” Field said.

Appellate public defense offers opportunities to reshape the law on a structural level. And experience is critical for achieving wins with big impacts like Blake and Gregory, Link said, pointing out that it took many years before WAP was able to achieve such results.

“The one thing appeals can do is, and this is true to a very lesser degree in trial court, but appellate courts have the ability to shape the law,” Link said. “They have the ability to say this is what the law actually means, and this is what the law actually allows, in a way that's just not possible anywhere else.”

As a trial public defender himself, Field said he relies on the work of appellate public defenders to do his own work. And with WAP’s critical mass of lawyers experienced in appellate work who can collaborate on and check each other’s work while training the next generation, WAP has worked on a lot of the cases Field depends on to defend his clients today. Field thinks the loss of WAP would have wide-reaching ramifications to the quality of justice indigent people in Washington receive.

“We’re not going to be able to rely on the kind of high quality appellate advocacy that has resulted in the life-changing decisions like Blake, like Gregory, that allow us to advocate effectively at the trial court level,” Field said. “The flow of those decisions will be disrupted and we will probably see fewer critical cases like that that made such a huge difference at our level.”

Field also worries that if WAP closes its doors, new lawyers might be discouraged from pursuing public defense appellate law. Combined with the Washington state legislature’s decision earlier this year not to dedicate some of the new revenue from the millionaires tax to public defense, attorneys might not want to practice in an area of law that it appears the state’s leadership doesn’t value.
Meanwhile, the legal staff at WAP face an uncertain future.

“These are talented lawyers, paralegals, legal assistants who are dedicated to public defense,” Johnson said. “We are very concerned about their future ability to work being so impacted by their director's decision on accountability.”

The next court hearing of the WAP suit will be on Friday, November 6, when the court is set to consider dispositive motions. If the judge grants either side’s summary judgment motion, the case will most likely come to an end.

articles.title: 7 stories on 12th Ave, 10 on the Starbucks Roastery site, and now the neighborhood Goodwill — This developer has big plans for Capitol Hill apartment projects
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A massing rendering for the Goodwill site (Image: PCP)

Another sign of thawing conditions for Seattle’s development freeze could be happening on Belmont Ave E where the building and parking lot home to the neighborhood’s Goodwill has been sold for $13 million to a developer holding a massive chunk of Capitol Hill’s future in its hands.
For now, the store remains open and serving the neighborhood where it opened in spring 2014 and replaced what had been Half Price Books .

This week’s sale puts the property in the hands of PCP , an Ohio-based development firm that typically specializes in build and hold, mixed-use developments focused on up-market amenities and finishes. In recent years, PCP has aggressively pushed outside the Rust Belt into Western mountain and Pacific Northwest markets.
On Capitol Hill, the company is positioning itself as a key driver in the neighborhood’s next wave of redevelopment.
PCP’s Capitol Hill holdings include 1208 E Olive where the 12th Ave property formerly to the Car Tender auto business has been cleared for eventual development of this 7-story project .
The massing concept for the company’s planned Starbucks Roastery redevelopment (Image: PCP)

PCP’s Capitol Hill crown jewel project could come on an even more high profile site. The company touts a plan for a 10-story mixed-use project on the site of the former Starbucks Roastery at Pike and Melrose as part of its Seattle portfolio.

The not-yet-public project has no filings with the city but PCP describes it as a “10 story multifamily development in the heart of Seattle’s Capitol Hill neighborhood” planned for 174 units across a 115,000-square-foot building “with over 10,000 SF of amenity space.”

Any sale agreement or contract related to the site is also not yet public. The county still records the 1920-era building and property as remaining in the hands of its longtime ownership, Weiss-Jenkins Properties .

In commercial real estate and private development pipelines, it is common practice for firms to list properties on their website under “Pipeline” or “Land” long before any deed transfer or city permit appears in public records.
Coffee giant Starbucks abruptly shuttered the showcase roastery in September 2025 . The building has remained empty since.

Goodwill’s Belmont store will be open and bustling this Thursday but change is coming. Six years ago, CHS reported on early planning for a mixed-use project for the site and preparation for a sale of the property. Those plans have grown.

PCP says it plans to develop the project as a 22,551-square-foot site that will demolish the old Goodwill store and a 4-unit small residential building on the property to make way for an 8-story, 172-unit apartment community.
Rendering of the 12th Ave project (Image: PCP)

The Belmont Ave Goodwill project is positioned as a premier, luxury market-rate development targeting high-income urban renters rather than a dedicated income-restricted affordable housing community. PCP emphasizes a high-end, “best-in-class” product intended to capture rental demand from professionals tied to the nearby First Hill medical hub, downtown Seattle, and regional tech employers via light rail.

During pre-development, the site’s commercial and residential tenants will generate approximately $44,000 per month in interim operating revenue, subsidizing land-loan interest ahead of demolition, PCP says.
PCP says the permitting process has been underway and that the Master Use Permit review covering zoning, civil engineering, SEPA, and design review is projected to require roughly 18 months.

The company’s announcement describes urgency to strike while the iron is hot. “PCP’s development strategy is intended to take advantage of the improving Seattle economy at a time where construction starts have dropped over 80% below the historical high mark,” the firm says.

articles.title: Police raises, less civilian response: What could really grow and shrink in Seattle’s 2027 budget
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Spending on SPD recruiting is one key pivot point in the city’s efforts to avoid a deficit

The Seattle City Council will find itself hemmed in by financial reality, left with little room to maneuver beyond Mayor Katie Wilson’s 2027–2028 proposed budget to eliminate a looming $175 million deficit, according to analysis presented Thursday at City Hall .
Thursday’s council budget committee session is focused on Seattle Police, CARE, Seattle Fire, the Unified Care Team, and the Human Services Department’s financial outlooks under the Wilson plan.
Closing the city’s budget gap without gutting core services leaves council representatives few alternatives to the mayor’s balancing blueprint.
There are hardcoded major spending increases in key areas in the plan.

Analysis being presented Thursday shows SPD funding would climb 13.9% to $556.5 million in 2027. $57.7 million of that increase is locked into base expenditures to fund union agreements with the Seattle Police Officers Guild , the Seattle Police Management Association , and parking enforcement officers.

Because these labor costs are legally fixed, Wilson’s budget tries to wrestle fiscal control by capping funded sworn staffing at 1,250 full-time equivalents, yielding 43 net hires in 2027 before freezing any planned increases in 2028.
Under the plan, deployable personnel would plateau at roughly 1,125 by 2029 as trainees graduate.

With student officers clogging the training pipeline and contract terms barring mandatory field-trainer assignments, attempting to accelerate hiring would balloon ongoing costs by tens of millions of dollars that the city cannot afford, department officials say. The council must likely also lean into the mayor’s civilian trims including cutting commercial ad campaigns, pausing hiring bonuses, and shelving vacant civilian detective and parking enforcement roles.

Council members face a similarly limited landscape in the Seattle Fire Department . Department analysis details Wilson’s proposed $7.1 million reduction to firefighter overtime, a 17% cut designed to curb ballooning operational deficits. To balance the ledger, the council must accept the administration’s plan for “unit outages,” lowering daily minimum staffing from 222 to 209 firefighters and temporarily taking engines out of service.

Seattle’s celebrated but hamstrung alternative response initiatives are also capped in the proposal. Analysis from the Community Assisted Response and Engagement department documents that saving $3.4 million requires cutting funding for 14 vacant Community Crisis Responders and eight 911 dispatchers.
The cuts would delay 24/7 dual-responder operations and cap service at 19 hours daily while shifting $6.3 million in gun violence prevention oversight from HSD to CARE.

Seattle’s homelessness response also faces a tight pathway. Analysis from the Human Services Department documents Wilson’s revenue redirection with General Fund allocations dropping 24% and backfilled by JumpStart payroll tax allocations from $2.4 million to $67.5 million to sustain 960 shelter beds and absorb 117 homelessness contracts back from the King County Regional Homelessness Authority .

The council will also weigh cuts to the city’s Unified Care Team, the multi-department effort tasked with addressing unsanctioned encampments and clearing public spaces. Wilson’s plan would reduce the team’s funding by $2.1 million (6.9%) and reduces authorized personnel by 9.3% from 113.5 to 105 FTE. Wilson’s plan cuts or transfers 10.5 positions across three departments, eliminating two vacant posts and $330,000 at HSD, cutting two vacant roles and pausing two more at SDOT, and eliminating 2.5 positions while shifting two equipment operators to Natural Resources at Seattle Parks and Recreation.

The UCT analysis reports that because these targets are mostly administrative, analytical, or advisory rather than frontline staff, the trims reflect an executive “right-sizing” that is unlikely to reduce daily encampment work.

The department analysis sessions are part of the build-up toward the council’s budget amendments and final approval of a spending plan. CHS reported here on Wilson’s proposal which would wipe out an inherited $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves. The proposal would cut roughly $50 million annually in General Fund spending by eliminating 128 positions and aligning departmental budgets with historical costs, pairing these cuts with $50 million in shuffled funding — primarily leveraging JumpStart payroll tax revenues to cover core services and homelessness programs — and enabling the city, Wilson says, to project balanced budgets through 2030 without drawing on reserves.
With every option stretched thin, the council’s options seem to be following Wilson’s roadmap or risking shortfalls across the city’s most elemental service.
The council amendment process will stretch out over the coming weeks.
A final “all-day” public hearing on the budget is scheduled for November 5th .

articles.author: Mitch Borden
paras: One seat is up for grabs on Seattle’s city council in this election, representing neighborhoods in the northernmost part of the city.

Affordability and public safety are top among the issues in the race. The special election is happening because city council member Cathy Moore resigned in 2025. Debora Juarez was appointed to fill the seat since then but did not run in this election.

Nilu Jenks and Julie Kang emerged as the top two candidates in the August primary, with Jenks receiving more than half of the votes. The winner will only fill the seat for the last year of Moore’s term before facing re-election in 2027.

Jenks is a political director for nonprofit FairVote Washington. She says food deserts in the area are a concern after Lake City lost its only full-service grocery store in 2025. That’s part of what prompted her to run.
“I’m running because I think blue cities should show that they can govern and meet our needs: Public safety, transportation, housing, shelter, but also really basic infrastructure,” she said.
Jenks received the endorsements of the Stranger, the King County Democrats and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay.
Kang is a college instructor and says she heard a clear message while out canvassing with voters.

“People just want the basics to work,” she said. “Safe streets, vibrant parks, clean neighborhoods. These are not things that are gonna cost a lot of money, or it's out of the extraordinary. These are the basics.”
Kang was endorsed by the Seattle Times, City Councilmember Bob Kettle and former Council President Sara Nelson.
Both candidates acknowledge the limits to what they can do in a year. They both say, if they were elected, they would run for re-election to a full four-year term next fall.

articles.title: Free Will Astrology
articles.author: Rob Brezsny
paras: ARIES (March 21-April 19): Before Aries-born Maya Angelou became a celebrated author, she was San Francisco’s first Black female streetcar conductor, a calypso dancer, a cook, a journalist in Ghana, and an actress. She didn’t publish her first memoir until she was 41. She spoke six languages and refused to believe that any single identity could contain her. I offer her as your role model in the coming weeks, Aries. It’s time to celebrate the wondrous truth that you don’t have to be just one thing. In fact, the astrological omens suggest you’ll thrive by rejoicing in the many disparate selves you are and have been and imagining new ones you might like to add. How kaleidoscopic do you dare to be? TAURUS (April 20-May 20): Here’s a hypothesis worth entertaining: You don’t fully know everything you want. Not yet. Not at the core, where desire isn’t well-behaved but turns wild and intense. Your fluency with surface desire can sometimes keep you from excavating the mysteries that live below it. The familiar longings override the stranger, stronger ones that haven’t found their bearings. So there are aspects of your primal yearnings that remain unexamined, simply because they require a particular stillness and courage to unearth completely. The good news: Now is an unusually favorable time to go looking.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20): Is your mental agility a gift or curse? It depends on whether you use it to avoid taking a stand or else deepen your understanding. In the coming weeks, Gemini, I hope you will practice the cagey skill of holding multiple truths simultaneously without letting that multiplicity become an excuse for never choosing or never committing. The goal is to encourage your magnificent mind to serve your heart rather than to override its tender wisdom. I love it when you unleash your clever analysis and it doesn’t devolve into sophisticated evasion. CANCER (June 21-July 22): Astronomers searching for planets around distant stars rarely see the planets directly. Instead, they notice tiny wobbles in the stars or faint dips in their brightness as the planets pass in front of them. You can and should practice a similar art now. Dramatic evidence may be unavailable, so watch for subtle shifts in mood, timing, synchronicity, and atmosphere. Small disturbances may reveal important hidden influences. Your most useful discoveries won’t come from looking harder but from noticing more gently. LEO (July 23-Aug. 22): Glassblowers repeatedly place molten glass into blazing furnaces as they shape it. They don’t heat it once and expect it to stay pliable forever. Again and again, they return it to the fire so new possibilities become available. This reminds me of the current chapter of your life story, Leo. Emotional intensity keeps recurring, repeatedly returning you to the heart of the heat and pressure. This may sometimes feel like a test or ordeal, but I think it’s the best way for you to master the crucial lessons and ensure the healing transformations. Be patient as you forge your masterpiece.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22): Master storytellers know that memorable heroes are admired because they continue moving despite uncertainty. Courage entails a resilient and affectionate partnership with doubt. I hope you’ll remember this if your confidence temporarily flickers in the coming weeks. There’s no need to waste precious energy trying to eliminate every hesitation before taking your next meaningful step. Let your questions accompany your convictions. They may sharpen your judgment. The coming weeks favor brave, thoughtful action, not flawless self-assurance.

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22): One morning soon, I predict you will open your inner eyes as well as your outer eyes and discover that you feel freer than you have in ages. Old specters that once pestered you will seem strangely powerless. Worn-out customs will have loosened their hold, and an ancient obligation will finally be settled. By some grace that neither you nor I can quite explain, at least some of the chains you fashioned in your own mind will have fallen away. What then? Celebrate! Host a personal “Out of Captivity” party, and give yourself a day or two to revel in your newfound liberty. Once you’re ready to make purposeful use of that delightful independence, ask yourself: “Where in my life do I most need a clean beginning?”

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21): Not so long ago, you got hints and clues that you were on the verge of getting a taste of tantalizing and off-limits treats. Weren’t you ready to accept when the invitation suddenly dissolved? And by now, haven’t you nearly stopped expecting to enjoy another chance? Then imagine your surprise if that temptation winds its way back to you soon. When you finally take a bite, it may taste and feel nothing like you anticipated. The wisest move will be to let go of your old assumptions and welcome the experience as it is. My prediction: You’ll be delightedly surprised by how deeply and sweetly it alters the way you understand reality—even if at first it feels disorienting.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21): Your upcoming challenges call to mind a feat once accomplished by conservationist and entertainer Steve Irwin. No, you won’t, as he did, feed a huge crocodile by hand while holding an infant in your other arm. But you may need to bring together qualities that seem at odds: fierceness and tenderness, a wild spirit and a protective instinct, boldness and love. Luckily, I am very sure you will summon the power and flair to do that.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19): Ecologists have found that transition zones, like where forests meet meadows or where land meets water, can support high biodiversity. They may include species from both neighboring habitats as well as species adapted to the distinctive conditions in the boundary zone. I propose we make these places your power metaphor for the coming weeks, Capricorn. You, too, can flourish in edge habitats. Instead of feeling compelled to choose one identity, community, philosophy, or style, appreciate your role as a translator between worlds. Your greatest gifts may emerge because you refuse to belong exclusively to any single camp. Revel in your fertile in-between-ness.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18): After pondering what might bring fresh vigor to your love life, I’ve arrived at an audacious suggestion: Offer a smoldering prayer while making love to a saintly soul in a place you regard as sacred. If that combination proves impractical, try just one or two parts of it: Pray wildly during an intimate encounter; flirt with or even seduce a person of uncommon goodness; kiss and hug and cuddle in a setting that feels holy to you; or speak to the divine in a titillating language you wouldn’t use in a formal religious service. The point is to let sensual delight and spiritual longing meet rather than keeping them apart.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20): You sometimes regard pleasure like a reward you have to earn through suffering, as if joy were a luxury item requiring payment in pain. But I have an alternate theory: Relaxed glee and earthy enjoyments are essential nutrients that are key to your health. So in my view, denying yourself beauty and comfort depletes you. I hope you will heed my guidance in the coming weeks, which is to treat yourself to almost more fun, happiness, bliss, and amusement than is allowed by law. See if you can break all previous records for rejuvenating delectation. New law of your universe, at least for the next four weeks: The quest for jovial gusto and zesty zeal are mandatory aspirations.

articles.title: Seattle Mayor Wilson’s First ‘Periodic Off-Topic’ Media Huddle
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: A mere 284 days into her tenure, Mayor Katie Wilson sat down with reporters to address a taboo subject: what Seattleites actually want to know.

Aside from a bit of FIFA-related bliss, Wilson has had a terrible summer. She’s been under a microscope for not being transparent enough, especially after the Bite of Seattle shooting. The numbers and specificity of Candidate Wilson have haunted Mayor Wilson.
We’ll get to that. But first, I wanted to know, why did she decide to do this now?

I tried to allude to this in my question to the mayor about why she was finally entering the off-topic media trenches. First, I thought of the Brazilian TV show Roda Viva (Roundtable Live) where politicians wade into a literal pit of criticism . Searching for something more familiar, I thought of the disgraced and clownishly corrupt former mayor who preceded Zohran Mamdani.

When I covered New York City, I used to dip into the weekly Tuesday press conference of Eric Adams, a jubilant spin zone where he’d take on his critics with rizz and occasional apparent lies. I mentioned this to Wilson as I put the question to her.
“I don’t know if that is a recommendation or not,” she said with a laugh.
“Can you talk a little bit about [why at] this point in your political career you decided to hold regular off-topics, and how you see it as a tool, and why you didn’t want to do it before?” I asked.

“It’s not that I didn’t want—” Wilson started. She began again. “This is something that we’ve actually talked about the possibility of really since the beginning. There’s just a lot that goes into standing up a mayor’s office and get rolling [ sic ] and so just we’re at the point now where that seemed like a good thing to introduce.”
Like former Seattle Mayor Bruce Harrell, Adams organized his pressers in a TV-friendly podium-facing-pews style. Harrell only trotted out the format when he thought he had good news, though.

Wilson’s staff had reorganized the executive reception area of her office with a classroom vibe, her and the press sitting around a table (in the style of outgoing New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat who has actually done something radical about childcare access). They described the Tuesday roundtable as part of a “periodic” availability to underscore the mayor’s commitment to transparency.

But there’s no guarantee that her staff will take up that effort again. As she’s done on progressive tax revenue, support for police, and homeless sweeps, we must ask if she’ll revert to a Harrellian instinct on media availability. “Periodic” is yet to be defined.
For months, Wilson has tried to ignore reporter questions about the issues of the day like shootings and progressive taxation under the maxim of “ let’s keep it on the topic of this event .”
It’s an excuse many mayors use to keep the media focused on various dog and pony shows, but it carries a bit more weight when they actually respond to media questions on other days.

On Tuesday, I saw one reason why it’s tempting to ignore questions, as members of the media asked her various iterations of Why hasn’t your police department caught the Bite of Seattle shooter??? It’s a question she could be asked at every event for months with answers that are largely out of her hands. (On Tuesday, she said—I’m paraphrasing here—cops are working hard, I’m impatient too, I’m giving them plenty of money, and—a real quote—“I’m assuming there will be a Bite of Seattle next year.”)

No wonder New York’s Mamdani didn’t continue his predecessor’s off-topic availability. It’s tough. Each week, he saves himself from a round in the octagon with my former colleagues at the New York Post .
But I also saw the value of her communication on Tuesday

Many Wilson supporters may have gotten the impression from her budget, and the accompanying budget speech, that she’s pushed progressive taxation down her priority list somewhere near colonizing Mars. Unlike Mamdani, she has no concrete proposal to tax the rich or increase overall spending for citizens outside law enforcement.
But in Tuesday’s presser, Wilson suggested she’s actually working on making something happen next year with the Legislature’s help.

“We are in active conversation with state legislators about the upcoming session and about bills that they’re interested in putting forward, and some of that includes revenue bills, whether that’s state level revenue bills or bills that would give cities like Seattle new revenue authority,” she said.
My doubts ( Is Mayor Katie Wilson Still a Socialist? ) are ever-so-slightly soothed. We’ll see where progressive revenue lands on her legislative priority list, but at least it’s an update.
And we’ll see if “periodic” gets as loosely defined as “socialism.”

articles.title: Trump should fear the BBC. Instead he’s picked a fight – and he seems to be losing | Emma Brockes
articles.author: Emma Brockes
paras: The president is used to bullying his media targets. The quagmire that is his libel actions shows the broadcaster is working to a different script

For the greatest account of the BBC’s finest hour, one must turn to Penelope Fitzgerald’s novel, Human Voices, written in 1980 and set 40 years earlier, at the corporation’s Portland Place wartime HQ. Flanked by sandbags and infused with a smell of cooking “from the deep hold that suggested more strongly than ever a cruise on the Queen Mary”, the organisation that Fitzgerald describes is at once noble and deeply eccentric. “Broadcasting House stood headed on a fixed course south,” she writes. “With the best engineers in the world, and a crew varying between the intensely respectable and barely sane, it looked ready to scorn any disaster.”

In other words, a formidable foe, one that in the spring of 1940, in the face of anticipated Nazi invasion, decided “without prompting, that truth was more important than consolation, and, in the long run, would be more effective”. I bring this up in respect to the gathering storm of Donald Trump versus the BBC, a fight triggered by the US president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit – $10bn! It’s a wonder he didn’t go for $10 gazillion – brought against the corporation at the end of last year in response to a poorly edited episode of Panorama. The BBC was at fault, editing together comments made by the US president at a rally on 6 January 2021 to give, as the corporation’s apology put it, “the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action”. But it is fighting the lawsuit.

articles.title: ‘Don’t do this!’ Why Paul McCartney cares about looking shorter than John Lennon in Sam Mendes’ Beatles films
articles.author: Stuart Heritage
paras: You’re Paul McCartney. So how come you’re still getting het up at a fictional version of you being marginally smaller than a fictional version of John Lennon?

There has been a lot of discourse and conjecture surrounding Sam Mendes’s forthcoming Beatles biopics. Some of this is logical (will people really turn out to see four near-identical films on the same day?), some creative (what animal did they have to shave to make John Lennon’s Abbey Road beard?). At every turn the film has been examined and factchecked and cross-referenced against testimonies from the band’s actual hairdresser .

But until now the remaining Beatles have managed to keep fairly quiet about the whole thing. Last year Ringo Starr mentioned that he’d sat down with Mendes to rework a scene he wasn’t happy with, and Paul McCartney has praised the guitar playing of Paul Mescal, but it appeared that no real red lines had been crossed. Until now.

articles.title: Gen Z wrestle with shame from ordering delivery food: ‘This economy is not for the weak’

paras: As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience

When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”

Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”
