articles.title: Using light to control brain cells – neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth explains how he made his Nobel-winning discovery
articles.author:
<name>Karl Deisseroth, D. H. Chen Professor, Professor of Bioengineering and of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Stanford University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/karl-deisseroth-2770199"/>
paras: The 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine honored Karl Deisseroth , Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work developing optogenetics – a technique that allows researchers to control the activity of neurons with light.

The Conversation Weekly podcast talked to Karl Deisseroth, a neuroscientist at Stanford University, about his journey developing optogenetics and its potential to treat a wide range of neuropsychiatric conditions. What follows is an edited transcript of the podcast.
Take us back to the early 1990s. You’re training to be a doctor and you start a rotation working with psychiatric patients. What questions about the brain did that raise for you?

Both basic neuroscience (people asking how the brain works) and clinical neuroscience (doctors trying to help people with brain disorders) have faced a very similar problem, which is the brain is quite mysterious and quite hard to study.

It’s billions of fragile, transparent, very fast-acting cells, buried within the skull and doing very complex things. We don’t have a good model for how the brain works, unlike the heart, which is very obviously a pump . We don’t actually know what the brain’s trying to do.

A lot of neuropsychiatric treatments are not as effective as they could be , and developing new ideas has been hard. The treatments we had were not grounded in a solid understanding of the cells involved. What are the cells actually doing? What are they trying to do? This was a problem that held back treatment.
When I was in psychiatry training in the early 2000s, and also as a medical student in the late 1990s, I was very much impressed with the magnitude of the challenge.
You went on to get a Ph.D. in neuroscience, and then you set up a lab at Stanford trying to understand how to control particular cells in the brain. What were the first experiments you did?
I have a background in molecular biology, and I knew how to work with genes. So I was motivated to see if we could use genetics to make a treatment or an intervention that targets one kind of cell.

Every cell has genes that tell it what to do. Different cells in the brain, just as other parts of the body, can be genetically targeted because different cells have different jobs. A cell that is a dopamine neuron has all the machinery needed to make the hormone dopamine. It uses different genes than a cell that makes the hormone serotonin, so they can be distinguished from each other.

And so the thought was maybe I could have a way of controlling just the dopamine cells or just the serotonin cells by inserting a specific gene into them. But I didn’t know what would work well, so I tried inserting different types of genes into neurons.

Some of the genes I tried were quite conventional; they were genes from mammals that I thought might affect the activity of neurons. But one was a gene from a single-celled algae – a microbe that converts light to energy. This gene coded for a light-activated protein called channelrhodopsin-2 that Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel identified a few years earlier.
And I thought it was worth a try. It was the least likely to work, but why not try it?
And amazingly, that was the one that worked. The genes that were lower risk didn’t work, and this gene from a single-cell microbe actually did.
Walk us through what you did. You inserted the gene into rat cells, right?

I had a preparation of cultured rodent neurons in a dish – basically a 24-well plate that let me look at many different conditions at the same time in different wells of this plate. This let me test side by side the conventional mammalian genes and this gene from the algae.
So the first step was to get the genes into the cells. Then I exposed some plates of cells to light, while others I did not. I used a test to see which cells had activated.

When I looked across the cells in the screen, I found that the ones that had the algae gene and had gotten light were showing this marker of activation, whereas the others had a much lower signal. That was a really thrilling moment because it showed that this gene from a photosynthetic single-celled organism – almost as far as you can possibly be from mammals evolutionarily – was working beautifully in fragile mammalian neurons.
It was a moment of a lot of pressure and complexity, but also delight.
Listen to Karl Deisseroth on The Conversation Weekly podcast .

You went on to name your method optogenetics – the ability to control specific nerves using light in the brain – and you soon went on to using it to control living mice in various ways. What was it like in those first few years of working with live animals?

The first experiment was in 2004 , but we didn’t show that it could control the behavior of freely moving mammals until 2007. So it took almost three years. But that first moment in 2007 was quite uplifting because that showed we had gone a big, big chunk of the way toward making it work.

This was an experiment that was very visible and easy to understand. The right side of the brain controls the left side of the body and attention to the left side of the world. We put in a fiber optic into the right part of a mouse motor cortex – the part that controls movement – and when we flipped the switch, the mouse immediately began going left in circles.
And then as soon as we turned off the laser light, it stopped and just looked up at us, as if nothing had happened.
That, coupled with the first experiment – those were transcendent moments.
What changed in your understanding of the brain in the moment you were able to switch particular neurons on and off?

We understood that the technique would probably work to help us understand the brain better at that moment. And then we immediately started applying it to all sorts of different cells where things were mysterious – where nobody knew or couldn’t prove exactly what one cell type or another was doing in perception and cognition and action.

We were able to find cells that were involved in hunger and thirst – basic survival drives. We were able to identify cells and pathways controlling aggression and defensiveness , parenting , how all the different parts of anxiety come on together and go away together, memory , motivation .
The general applicability became clear over the subsequent years.
Researchers are now using optogenetics in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. How does that work?
In 2010, two of my colleagues in Europe were interested in delivering one of these light-activated proteins to human eye samples – specifically the retina of the eye – which worked very well.

So they did careful studies in monkeys and in people. And in 2021, just five years ago, they published a paper showing they could confer light sensitivity back to the retinas of a person who was completely blind from a neurodegenerative disease called retinitis pigmentosa .
That’s what we call direct optogenetics . It’s somewhat complicated because you have to deliver the gene and light to the person.
And going back to your psychiatric patients, who you still see in the clinic today, how do you hope optogenetics will be able to help them?

There’s a much easier and more broadly impactful avenue that we call indirect optogenetics , which uses the knowledge that comes from studying which cells matter in a symptom and then designing medications that target those cells. This is something we’ve really lacked in neuropsychiatry for a long time.
Indirect optogenetics is making strong headway for autism and schizophrenia . There are trials that are moving to their final stages for those disorders.
My particular clinical specialty is autism, and I see the difficulties that come with irritability and anxiety in these patients. And I can see optogenetics leading to new medications that will help.
Karl Deisseroth has received funding from the NIH and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. He was the founder of MapLight Therapeutics, a biopharmaceutical company.

articles.title: As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?
articles.author:
<name>Murugan Anandarajan, Professor of Decision Sciences and Management Information Systems, Drexel University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/murugan-anandarajan-2404641"/>
paras: Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.
But does the employee know how to do the task?

I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.

AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.

The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not.
What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.

The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance – rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.

This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.

More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ ironies of automation ”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem.
This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.

What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.

Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control.

This creates a mismatch. Research on meaningful human control suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility and capability can begin to separate.
Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.

Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as accuracy and productivity . Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps.

But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The number of overrides alone tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.

The key is to understand how the division of work between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.
Organizational governance – defining roles and responsibilities – is also under pressure from AI.

Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to change over time . There is nothing inherently wrong with that change.

The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?
In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic.

Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.

Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.

As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.
For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?

articles.title: Americans who go to church and trust science are also more likely to believe in ghosts and curses, new research shows
articles.author:
<name>Ruiqian Li, Research Assistant Professor at the School of Public Affairs, American University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/ruiqian-li-2761926"/>
paras: Americans who trust science and reason more than their churches’ teachings, but still believe in God or attend services, are also more likely to believe in magic than those who prioritize religious teachings.

This was the central finding of a study my co-authors and I published in the journal Social Forces in July 2026. We analyzed the latest wave of the Baylor Religion Survey , a nationally representative survey of 1,812 American adults that Gallup fielded in early 2025.

We used four of its questions to measure an outlook we call “secular rationalism.” The term refers to the belief that science is the only way to understand the world and that morality should rest on reason rather than religious teachings. Secular rationalism also includes the idea that people should interpret spiritual matters on their own rather than trust religious authorities.

We looked at people who embrace secular rationalist ideas but also believe in the supernatural. We asked respondents how strongly they believed in six things that people often call magic and require no god or church, from ghosts and curses to talking to the dead. For comparison, we also measured belief in miracles, such as whether miracles still happen today and whether God is the source of all miracles.

What’s interesting was that people who scored high on “secular rationalism” beliefs were more likely to believe in magic, so long as they kept some tie to religion. Among Americans who believe in God, those who also agree with secular rationalism were about twice as likely to lean toward magic as those who reject secular rationalism – 40% vs. 19%. Among people who attend religious services, the share was 28% vs. 19%. Among people who never attend services or do not believe in God, secular rationalism was no longer linked to belief in magic.

Some of the groups we compared were small. According to Baylor Religion Survey 2025 data, fewer than 1% of Americans neither believe in God nor generally agree with these secular rationalist ideas but actively reject them, while about 18% believe in God and agree with them.

Some people may still show up to church, or still believe in God, yet no longer grant their church the authority to define their belief about the supernatural. In short, our research shows, magic thrives where individual rationality and spirituality meet.

About 3 in 10 American adults now claim no religious affiliation . Scholars are still debating whether the decline of organized religion will also mean the decline of belief in the supernatural in the U.S. A long tradition of social theory predicts that as religious institutions decline, a scientific outlook with no room for supernatural or magic will take its place.

Our findings suggest that many Americans who no longer affiliate with an organized religion may still believe in tarot, astrology or psychic services. More broadly, most Americans without a religion still hold some spiritual belief. According to the Pew Research Center , 29% of Americans have no religion, but only 5% call themselves atheists. Most say their religion is “nothing in particular,” and two-thirds of that group still believe in something beyond the natural world.

Why are we seeing this trend? As French sociologist Emile Durkheim wrote in 1912, “ The magician has a clientele, not a church .” Magic needs no congregation, clergy or theology, so believers can adopt it without leaving their church. That makes magic a natural fit for people who still believe in God but no longer let institutions define the supernatural for them. It may also explain its appeal to younger Americans, who distrust institutions most and, as our data suggests, are likely to believe in both magic and secular rationalism.

Our data comes from a single point in time. It shows that people who are religious but also trust science and reason are more likely to believe in magic. But it can’t tell us whether these people are drifting away from religion, coming back to it or staying where they are. To find out, we would need to survey the same people who participated in the original survey over time.

Archaeologist Chris Gosden argues that belief in magic is older than both religion and science, and for most of history it has existed side by side with religion. What our study adds is a clearer picture of when trust in science goes hand in hand with magic: among people who stay religious but no longer let their church decide what is true.
We still know little about how magical beliefs spread among young Americans, or why they appeal to them. Answering those questions is an important next step for research on belief.
The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work.

articles.title: Do you think teachers are similar to coaches, pastors or something else? It depends on where you live
articles.author:
<name>Gustavo E. Fischman, Professor of Education Policies and Comparative Studies, Arizona State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/gustavo-e-fischman-1133604"/>
paras: Three answers, three countries, one open-ended question: “Teaching is similar to what other occupation or activity?”
We asked this question to more than 3,000 people across the United States, England and Australia between May 2025 and March 2026.
Coaching was the front-runner across all three countries. But the similarities partially diverged there.

Respondents in England and Australia more often compared teaching with professional roles such as nursing and social work. U.S. respondents, meanwhile, more often likened teaching to being a parent and religious roles, such as a cleric or pastor.
In the three countries, however, one other idea stood out: Teaching was primarily associated with a caring relationship.
We have previously examined how Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. find common ground on what makes a good teacher, despite the polarization in the country on education and many other issues.
This time, we wanted to know whether people across countries had similar ideas of teachers.

In all three countries, respondents most often described teaching as centered in the relationship between teacher and student: a form of coaching, caregiving, parenting and other types of personal support.
Coaching was the most common answer in each country, but its prominence varied.
Coaching was named by 30% of U.S. respondents, compared with 23% in England and 23% in Australia.
The differences became more pronounced when participants named other occupations and activities.
Respondents in England and Australia were more likely to associate teaching with institutional, credentialed and paid professional roles, such as nursing, lecturing and social work.

“Nursing. They care for and look after people whilst they are at their most vulnerable. Teachers do a similar thing by caring and teaching young people some of the skills they will need later in life,” a 39-year-old Australian man told us.
“A lecturer, you are passing on knowledge to people, usually the younger generation,” another 32-year-old man in England said.

Compared with respondents in those countries, U.S. respondents were more likely to describe teaching through caregiving roles, such as parenting, and through religious figures, such as priests, pastors or rabbis.
“Being a parent, you are caring for young minds and shaping them through learning,” a 33-year-old woman in the U.S. told us.
“As a preacher, he teaches the word of God. How they deliver the word determines how well the people will understand it,” a 23-year-old woman in the U.S. said.

While international comparisons are informative, they do not represent a single view of teaching. Instead, they suggest that respondents in three countries likely drew on somewhat different cultural repertoires when describing the profession.
We were surprised by just how much agreement we found.

Despite differences in schooling models and cultural norms, people in the United States, England and Australia had remarkably similar ideas about how relationships are at the heart of teaching, closely echoing our other work showing that Republicans and Democrats view teachers similarly.
In September 2026, The New York Times conducted an informal survey of 37 education researchers who gave 30 ideas about how to fix schools.

Their list consists primarily of interventions such as more per-pupil funding, banning cellphones and restricting artificial intelligence in the classroom. These ideas appeared far less often in our participants’ explanations of what teaching resembles.
In fact, out of more than 3,000 responses to our survey, AI came up only a handful of times and never as the reason teaching and another occupation were said to be alike.
Given how central AI has become to political and academic debates about the future of education , its near-total absence in these public descriptions of teaching is notable.
At the same time, experts and citizens agree that what separates very good teaching from poor execution is likely the quality of the relationship between educators and children.

We think that serious conversation about student achievement must include clear descriptions of very good teachers: the practices they use to encourage and enable students to learn. Our research shows that teaching should make room for both the transmission of knowledge and the meaningful and caring relationships that make learning possible.

articles.title: Ketamine’s role in alleged Cornell rape highlights flood of psychoactive drugs on campus
articles.author:
<name>Christopher P. Holstege, Professor of Emergency Medicine and Pediatrics, University of Virginia</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christopher-p-holstege-731398"/>
paras: Former Cornell student Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit in September 2026 alleging that seven fraternity members raped her at a party, said the young men who assaulted her pressured her into taking the drug ketamine.

As an emergency room physician, medical toxicologist and the head of student health services at the University of Virginia, I have had a front-row seat to the growing danger that psychoactive substances such as ketamine present to the health and safety of university students.

Ketamine and its emerging spin-off versions are part of a wave of new and evolving designer drugs entering the United States and other countries. How widely these substances are used remains unknown, since most hospitals are unable to detect them on standard urine drug screens. But ketamine and other drugs are being increasingly reported as agents used in sexual assault – either when people take these drugs voluntarily, are pressured to take them or are given them covertly.
The increasing prevalence of ketamine and other drugs – and their use in sexual assault – is playing out on college campuses across the U.S. and putting students at risk.

Ketamine is a synthetic chemical that was first synthesized in 1962 . The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved it as a general anesthetic for people and animals in 1970, and doctors and veterinarians used it for decades to induce anesthesia during surgeries and to relieve pain.

People have used ketamine recreationally since the 1970s. Getting high on it became more popular in the U.S. in the 1980s, when it was called “Special K.” It was frequently found in the club drug scenes and was associated with raves into the 1990s. Today, ketamine is sold on the street under a variety of slang names , such as K, Ket, and Vitamin K.

In 2019, the FDA approved a nasal spray version of ketamine , called esketamine, to treat depression that does not respond to other treatments. That drug’s use is tightly regulated, but clinicians are increasingly prescribing ketamine “off-label” for a variety of psychiatric conditions, including post-traumatic stress disorder .

Cases of poisoning caused by ketamine in the U.S. doubled between 2019 and 2023 , according to an analysis of calls to poison control centers nationwide, and are now the highest they’ve ever been. This surge is in part due to the more widespread medical use of ketamine, which makes accessing it much easier. But street versions of the drug are also prevalent as chemists in basement laboratories create novel ketamine analogs.

Ketamine’s effects vary depending on the dose and the person. It can cause someone to dissociate, creating an altered state of consciousness, changing what’s perceived through the senses and causing a sense of detachment from one’s self and one’s surroundings. The drug can also cause coma at high doses .

Someone who orally consumes ketamine would typically begin to feel its effects within 20 minutes . If they inhale or inject it, the effects are almost immediate. The primary effects generally wear off in less than an hour, but a person’s senses may remain dulled and their judgment and coordination impaired for several hours afterward.

Ketamine can cause a slew of other side effects, including delirium, amnesia, increased salivation, abnormal eye movements, high blood pressure and potentially fatal breathing problems. Alcohol and other drugs can interact with ketamine to worsen these effects significantly.

Ketamine is generally sold illegally as either a colorless, odorless liquid or a white or off-white powder. Either form can be easily and covertly placed into an unsuspecting person’s beverage or food. Ketamine can be snorted, and it can be smoked or vaped on products such as marijuana.

Research is extremely spotty on how often a perpetrator of rape or sexual assault uses a chemical agent – whether ketamine, alcohol or another substance – to alter a victim’s senses. Research suggests that most often both parties use mind-altering substances voluntarily , although the effects of these substances can alter a person’s ability to grant consent.

Even so, there are numerous reports of perpetrators spiking a victim’s drink or otherwise slipping a drug to them without their knowledge. According to one study, 4.2% of rape victims were drugged covertly , though how often this actually happens is undoubtedly underreported.

That’s because it’s very hard to detect drugs taken this way. Most of the substances used to facilitate sexual assaults are rapidly absorbed and metabolized by the body, rendering them difficult to detect in routine urine and blood drug screenings. Another issue is that many days may have elapsed between the victim ingesting the drugs and their subsequent treatment at a medical facility.

Victims of rape or sexual assault are often reluctant to report incidents because of a sense of embarrassment, guilt or perceived responsibility, or because they may know their attacker. Some may not trust that their institution or local law enforcement will support them.

In my experience, the involvement of ketamine or other drugs invariably makes a bad situation worse – complicating consent, impairing judgment and reducing inhibitions. Ketamine causes confusion and drowsiness , and its sedative, hypnotic and memory-erasing properties can diminish a survivor’s recollection of events surrounding the sexual assault.

The availability of these drugs in the U.S., including on college campuses, has risen sharply – particularly since the early 2010s, as a slew of new substances have emerged and international drug control efforts have not kept up . Without more active education and prevention efforts, as well as better detection methods for these drugs, students will continue to pay the price.

articles.title: Why the GOP’s voter fraud messaging may backfire
articles.author:
<name>Christopher Miller, Visiting Assistant Professor of Philosophy, Politics, Economics, and Law (PPEL), University of Richmond</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christopher-miller-1541575"/>
paras: With Election Day 2026 just weeks away and control of Congress hanging in the balance, the results will almost certainly hinge on voter turnout, just as they did in 2024.

Given that genuinely undecided voters are scarce — as little as 5% to 7% of the electorate , according to major polls — both Democrats and Republicans must look to mobilize their rank-and-file supporters. To do so, the Republican Party has bet strongly this year on a strategy of convincing people that voter fraud is rampant .

As a scholar of U.S. politics , I see this as a high-risk strategy for Republican candidates and American democracy. That’s because reduced trust in election integrity can reduce motivation to vote – even if based on flawed information. But it’s not at all clear which Americans are most likely to stay home in November.

Voter fraud is not a real problem in the United States. Study after study, by public officials and think tanks , has shown that voting by noncitizens and other ineligible voters happens only at minuscule, statistically insignificant levels.

Nonetheless, rhetoric from the Trump administration about voter fraud has been pervasive. Consider the recent claim by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls – a number reduced to 185 when state authorities pressed for details, and reduced to zero when the state investigated the names provided.

There is comparable behavior from Congress. My own research on political communication has shown that a substantial number of members of Congress, strongly skewing Republican, make frequent use of rhetoric that undermines democratic norms and delegitimizes political institutions.

The strategy ties readily into President Donald Trump’s persistent false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election . It also ties into his administration’s strongly anti-immigrant agenda , which spreads fear of noncitizens corrupting U.S. politics .
How does this uncertain political environment influence voters?

There is clear data showing that voter confidence in elections has fallen across party lines: Only 65% of Republicans, 64% of Democrats and 57% of independent voters are very or somewhat confident that the 2026 vote count will be reliable. Conventional wisdom suggests such discouraging numbers would depress turnout.
Extensive research confirms the axiom that a sense of civic duty is the strongest predictor of whether someone will vote . It supersedes trust, partisanship and policy preferences.

Any campaign’s quest to mobilize additional voters, therefore, must find them among citizens without a strong sense of civic duty. But among these people, diminished trust in democratic processes can play out in counterintuitive ways.

Recent research on German voters is relevant to the U.S.: It shows that among more passive voters – those following cues from political elites – reduced trust in elections can depress motivation to vote. That’s because there’s no trustworthy result that voters are seeking to affirm.
Conversely, among voters with greater skepticism about elite messaging, reduced trust can motivate increased turnout as an attempted corrective for a flawed system.
What does this mean for potential voters in the U.S.? Among Republicans, it appears that the party’s strategy carries a strong risk of backlash.

Findings from MIT’s Election Lab confirm that cues from political elites are a powerful factor in voter behavior. Specifically, cues setting expectations of a disappointing or untrustworthy result will reduce motivation. Why vote if you don’t expect it to help achieve the desired result?

The same study finds Republican voters broadly inclined to believe GOP leaders’ cues about voter fraud and to frame their expectations accordingly. And once they’ve made that shift, they cling firmly to the belief , even in the face of contrary empirical evidence or messaging from within the party.

In the current election cycle, 50% of Republicans surveyed distrust mail-in voting, and 51% fear voting by noncitizens. They expect election results to be fraudulent. This likely won’t mobilize them, as there’s no positive result they can expect to affirm. The Republican Party’s messaging has painted its voters into a corner.

Democrats, meanwhile, are less inclined to believe claims of voter fraud. But they are more inclined to be concerned about attempts to undermine the midterms by political elites making such claims. Examples include the Trump administration’s efforts to sow doubt about voting by mail and about alleged noncitizen voting .

These efforts increase motivation to vote among Democrats. Unlike GOP voters, they see the capacity to correct for the system’s vulnerabilities – the potential and urgency to overwhelm attempts at voter suppression through higher turnout.

Opponents of Trump and the GOP may find these diverging effects encouraging. No matter the results this November, however, we’re left with a precarious dynamic. Increasing numbers of voters lack trust in elections and make their decisions to vote – or not – based on limited or flawed information.
Although voters in general are poorly informed about how elections are conducted, they can and do respond to clear information familiarizing them with election processes.

I’ve seen this myself over the years, working with nonpartisan efforts to register young adults and train them as poll watchers. And in the current election cycle, there have already been widespread efforts to broaden public awareness about the fact that state officials, not federal ones, have authority over voter rolls and election security.

Meanwhile, fewer Americans are expected to vote by mail this year – whether due to fear of fraud or fear of the Post Office . If they instead vote in person, a silver lining is that positive personal experiences with poll workers are also associated with increased voter trust.

Looking beyond November, what Americans can hope for is a cycle in which clear election outcomes provide an opportunity to inform voters of how and why the system works. That’s the way to motivate more political engagement and voter turnout in the future.

articles.title: 2026 General Election Endorsements
articles.author: Elections Committee
paras: This midterm election will be a big deal, and not just because Democrats could retake Congress from Republicans and provide a check on Trump’s power at the federal level. A ton of interesting races and measures are also brewing at the local level. Ballots should be arriving in mailboxes by October 16 across Washington state.

It’s imperative that we block megamillionaire Brian Heywood’s latest Eymanesque effort to hijack Washington state’s legislative process through ballot initiative campaigns he and his rich friends bankroll. Their top goal this session seems to be to repeal the millionaires tax, and the benefit to them is obvious. The question is what does lowering taxes on multimillionaires get the rest of us?

As a side quest to their tax the rich repeal battle, Heywood’s campaign also seeks to force schools to turn over kids’ medical records, even if they’re parents are charged with abuse. Plus, they want to inspect your kids’ genitals before they can play sports. This is in the name of the alleged scourge of trans women competing in school sports, but it’s a solution in search of a problem, with a massive amount of harmful side effects. Vote no on all three statewide initiatives from these creepy multimillionaires.

Meanwhile, Washington State’s congressional delegation did not exactly inspire us with confidence that they will be leading the charge to defang Trump, and too few long-time incumbents drew credible challenges. Further down the ticket, however, we see plenty of exciting candidates – some even daring to challenge powerful incumbents and force them to defend how they are adapting to our present political moment.

The progress being made in Olympia stands in stark contrast to intractable federal gridlock on key issues and increasing democratic backsliding. In a productive period from 2023 to 2025, state lawmakers phased out single family zoning in favor of more affordable middle housing, enacted rent stabilization, reformed parking mandates, and barred cities from broadly banning apartments near our biggest transit investments.
Find our endorsements useful? Donate to support our Election Committee's work and our local reporting that informs it.

The Washington State Legislature is fresh off passing a millionaires tax that will help ease the burden on the working class once it goes into effect in 2029. We were impressed by the broad coalition that advanced the tax, which only hits those who earn more than $1 million in compensation per year, and convinced Governor Bob Ferguson (hardly known for his boldness or backbone) to get behind the effort.

Unfortunately, after queuing up the millionaires’ tax, Ferguson has settled back into his lane of opposing new efforts to tax the rich and focusing the agenda on cuts to state programs. We do not think the work of progressive tax reform is done, and we want to see the state do more to invest in our future, whether expanding public transit, investing in affordable housing, ensuring universal health care, or meeting the state’s paramount duty to ensure the “ample provision for the education of all children.”

Our slate of candidates for the state House and Senate is ready to continue that work, and we’re excited to see what our state can accomplish when it sheds outmoded constraints, like a car-centric approach to infrastructure investments or an instilled fear of taxing the rich.

Oh and did we mention control of the Seattle City Council could also be up for grabs due to a special election in District 5? With centrists still holding a grip on council, progressive legislation continues to face a fraught path forward. Whether Mayor Katie Wilson gets a chance to deliver on campaign promises to make Seattle a more affordable and safe place to live could depend on electing progressive councilmembers, like Nilu Jenks, who [spoiler alert] we enthusiastically endorsed in the D5 race. Read on to see why.

Ballots should be arriving in your mail boxes this week. Washington voters have until 8pm Tuesday, November 3 to return a ballot at a drop box or get it postmarked. Visit the Vote WA portal to register or check your voter information.

The 2026 Elections Committee is led by chairs Forrest Baum and Kelsey Vanhee. Membership includes Tamer Abouzeid, Mike Bollich-Ziegler, Angela Compton, Austin Field, Caitlin Hepworth, Amber Hu, Naomi Lewis, Oliver Moffat, Ryan Packer, Maya Ramakrishnan, Jazmine Smith, and Doug Trumm.
Find our endorsements useful? Donate to support our Election Committee's work and our local reporting that informs it.
Urbanists will join the long list of groups voting “NO” on Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 (aka the “Parents’ Bill of Rights”).

Sadly, not all kids live in homes that are safe and accepting, and for some vulnerable kids, teachers and school counselors may be the only safe grownups in their lives. Right-wingers have long worked to dismantle public education and attack the educators and staff who work to protect victims of child abuse and LGBTQ+ kids.

Hedge fund manager Brian Heywood is back again trying to trick voters into passing his so-called “Parents’ Bill of Rights” — officially titled “Initiative Measure No. IL26-001.” This badly written initiative would force schools to involuntarily “out” LGBTQ+ kids and strip privacy from child abuse victims.

Voters might be wondering why this scrap of rage bait has risen again. A few years ago, Heywood’s Let’s Go Washington PAC hired signature gatherers to get the first “Parent’s Rights” initiative certified. That original version tried to trick voters into stripping student privacy protections by hiding it within a long list of already existing “Parental Rights”.

But the state legislature defused Heywood’s sneak attack by simply adopting all the duplicative rules while still protecting the privacy of vulnerable children. Now Heywood and his MAGA buddies have once more crawled from under a rock and hired signature gatherers to place their “Parental Rights” initiative back on the ballot.

Urbanists won’t be fooled: this initiative has nothing to do with protecting kids and families. If approved by voters, I-001 would force schools to turn over private records about child abuse victims to their parental abusers. Even parents under criminal investigation for sexual abuse of their child would gain access to private school counseling records.

By requiring schools to disclose highly confidential mental health counseling files to parents, I-001 forces school counselors to “out” vulnerable LGBTQ+ kids to their families. Because of family rejection, LGBTQ+ children (especially trans kids) are more likely to experience homelessness than other kids and are at higher risk of self-harm than other kids.
This cruel Initiative would strip kids’ privacy, causing family conflict, increased youth homelessness, and worsen the teen mental illness crisis. Vote “NO” on Initiative Measure No. IL26-001.

Mandatory sex inspections of young girls is not a phrase any of us wants to be writing, any of you want to be reading, or anyone should ever want to require. This initiative, bafflingly, claims to be about “defending equity in interscholastic sports” while prohibiting a tiny number of trans students from participating in sports and subjecting all girls to a mandatory inspection to confirm their biological sex.

Still need a reason to vote no? No Hate in Washington State calls I-638 “The most extreme MAGA measure of its kind in the U.S., I-638 would require tens of thousands of elementary, middle and high school girls (but not boys) to undergo intrusive, potentially harmful medical sex inspections every year as a new part of sports physicals.”

Call us old-fashioned, but we think youth sports are supposed to be about having fun, encouraging physical activity, teamwork, and leadership skills, not about unnecessary and invasive medical inspections or imposed gender conformity. We’re proud to join the Washington State PTA , the Washington Education Association , League of Women Voters , and many, many more in opposing this awful initiative. Vote no on I-638.

We’ve been screaming from the rooftops for years that if we want to get this state on track, we absolutely must fix our regressive, upside-down tax code. It’s also wildly popular and works like a charm . It’s why we support the capital gains tax and defended it when hedge fund manager Brian Heywood tried to repeal it in 2024. And it’s why the millionaires tax is another huge step forward in making meaningful change in our struggling state budget so that we can continue to have the way of life in Washington that people love.

Like the attempted capital gains tax repeal, this new attack on the millionaires tax would upend our budget if passed and defund our schools and healthcare. The ballot measure, listed as IP26-645, was forced onto the ballot by a multi-million-dollar signature-gathering campaign funded by Haywood and his rich friends, hoping to shrink their tax bills – even though the richest 1% already pay a lower tax rate than the vast majority of middle-class Washingtonians.

First, let’s get some facts straight. This tax is narrower than simply being a millionaire: the tax applies to income over a million dollars per year (less than 20,000 households) and would only apply after that millionth dollar. If you make $1,000,100 in one year, your tax burden would be $9.90.

Despite that narrow pool and large deduction, it’s projected to bring in over $3 billion per year to fund schools, child care, healthcare, and reduce/eliminate other taxes everyday people pay. In other words: with the millionaires tax, most people pay less in taxes, small businesses pay less in taxes, and the ultrawealthy pay a little bit more towards their fair share. Without it, we lose big on the things that matter most to us.

What would you do with a million extra bus hours? Well, the Seattle Transit Measure is investing them in more frequency, more weekend service, more midday service, and more late-night service. Plus, the transit measure would fund more free ORCA passes for low-income riders. This renewal would take all of the bonus investments that Seattle has infused into Metro service and amplify it, in addition to funding the streetcar system and more.

Everyone should be able to get to where they’re going at any time of day in a world-class city like Seattle. We deserve to be able to make it to the kids’ soccer games on weekends, make it home from a night out or a late shift, and have regular, frequent service throughout the day.

Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposal doubles the size of the transit measure, raising about $138 million annually by increasing the measure’s sales tax from 0.15% to 0.3%. That would give Seattle extra purchasing power, with 280,000 bus service hours to invest annually instead of the 180,000 previously. Seattle and Metro expect at least 10 of the city’s busiest buses to see augmented service over current levels.

Because this is a renewal of existing revenue, if the measure were to fail, we would lose funds, lose service hours, lose frequency, and lose big altogether. While sales taxes are regressive, cutting bus service is far more regressive.
Hop on board, Seattle. Vote Yes on Prop 1.

Just as critically, Pierce County absolutely must pass its own transit measure . It’s also a small sales tax increase, but it would similarly mean more buses, running to more places, more often. It also makes buses fare-free for seniors. So much good would come of the investments into Pierce Transit that this measure enables.
Prop 1 would increase service levels by more than 40%, a massive infusion for a county that has lagged behind on transit investment.

If approved, the ballot measure would bump the dedicated sales tax rate funding Pierce Transit from 0.6% to 0.9%, a funding stream that has been sitting unchanged since George W. Bush's first term in the White House. That would put Pierce County in closer parity with neighboring counties, which boast more frequent bus service.

With the added funding, Pierce Transit expects to be able to add four brand new routes across Tacoma and Puyallup, extend hours on 23 routes, and boost frequencies on 21 routes to run at least every 20 to 30 minutes on the weekends, compared to just four routes clearing that basic bar for frequency today.

When we think about how people get around, where they get around and how we can connect communities across the sound, Pierce has to be a part of that picture. It’s not just about Tacoma. Whether you live in Puyallup or Gig Harbor, Steilacoom or Fife, you deserve transit access and reliable service.

While Seattle often passes transit funding measures by comfortable margins, the same is not true of Pierce County, which saw its last transit measures fail in 2011 and 2012. It’s going to be a tight race to get it passed, so it’s important to vote yes and talk to your neighbors about how important it is that they do, too!

articles.title: Taru: Montlake coffee shop to become family-friendly cafe with built-in playscape
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: You can follow Shah’s journey opening Taru @filisha.shah

A Montlake coffee shop is getting a playful makeover. The neighborhood’s Fuel Coffee is becoming Taru , a hybrid cafe concept designed to serve both parents and little ones — “Coffee for you. Rumpus time for them.”

The reimagined space is spearheaded by entrepreneur Filisha Shah . “I live in the neighborhood and have a little one of my own,” Shah said. “On rainy Seattle mornings I kept wishing for a place with good coffee where she could play. So I’m making it here.”

The transformation comes as the Fuel Coffee family was put up for sale this summer as its ownership looked to transition out the industry. The 19th Ave E Fuel has become art-focused Inkling Art & Cafe while the small chain’s Ada’s Technical Books centerpiece remains shuttered and in search of new ownership on 15th Ave E.
In Montlake, Taru hopes to continue Fuel’s level of espresso and coffee service and will continue serving Stamp Act coffee at the same corner. But major additions are on the way.

Operating from morning into evening, Taru, which in Sanskrit and Hindi translates to “tree,” will branch out with a food menu with family-friendly bites and new additions like caffeine-free beverages and bubbly.

Inspired by family cafés in Amsterdam, Taru will feature “The Grove,” a custom wooden playscape built directly into the café that offers climbing structures and open-ended play for toddlers and young children. The Grove will be scaled for children aged 1 to 5 –though older siblings are welcome.

Montlake old-timers might chuckle at the idea. The old Montlake Alehouse that used to be part of the block across the street was infamous for its “play pit” area that became a de facto play area for kids though was originally designed as some kind of post-hippie carpeted lounge area. The owner of a tavern project that took over the space in the mid 2010s called it “kiddie Thunderdome” before ripping it out.
A decade and change later, the strong kids vibes are back in Montlake where recent commercial additions include a School of Rock music education studio.
But Taru’s new home has a history that includes delighting children. The former grocery building served as the Montlake branch of the Seattle Public Library until the early 2000s.
Taru is scheduled to open in late fall at 2300 24th Ave E. Learn more at tarucoffeeandplay.com .

articles.title: Five years of katsu on 15th Ave E: Kobuta & Ookami looks back, and north to Mountlake Terrace
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: When Kobuta & Ookami finally opened its doors on 15th Ave E in fall 2021, Sue Phuksopha wasn’t sure anybody would show up. The partners had signed their lease before COVID-19 shut everything down, then watched construction stall for months. When opening day came, they found a line waiting outside.
“After waiting so long and not knowing what was going to happen, seeing that line made us so happy and excited,” Phuksopha told CHS.

Five years later, the katsu specialist has grown into a small family of restaurants , Capitol Hill and Redmond today, with a third location planned for Mountlake Terrace in 2027. CHS caught up with the team to talk about what’s changed, what hasn’t, and why Seattle can’t seem to get enough fried pork cutlet.
The pandemic delay turned out to have a silver lining. Because rent didn’t kick in until the space was turned over, the partners used the extra months to refine recipes and the menu.

Opening was still a challenge. Kobuta & Ookami debuted as dine-in only at a time when people were still uneasy about sitting down inside a restaurant. Staff checked vaccination cards and worked to make both customers and employees feel safe.
“We thought we would have a little more time to adjust, but we had to learn very quickly,” Phuksopha said. “All of us as partners learned different positions and jumped in wherever we were needed.”
When the restaurant opened, Phuksopha told CHS they wanted to capture the casual street-dining vibe of the little alleys in Japan. That’s still the goal.

“When we travel there, we really love the little restaurants, the alleys, places under the train tracks, just sitting down with good food, sake, beer or a highball, spending time with friends and enjoying yourself,” Phuksopha said.

The team still travels to Japan at least once a year. “We like to call it ‘research,’ but really, we just love going there,” Phuksopha said, and they always come back with new ideas for food, drinks and atmosphere.

When it first opened, CHS marked Kobuta & Ookami as a first for the neighborhood. After years of mixed-use development bringing new buildings with brand new restaurant spaces to Capitol Hill, 2021 marked the beginning of the development slowdown. Kobuta & Ookami’s September debut was the first and one of the only food and drink debuts in a fresh restaurant space part of a new development that year.

The restaurant has become more than expected, with longtime regulars, families, visitors brought in by out-of-town friends, and customers who have followed them from Capitol Hill to Redmond. Phuksopha credits much of that growth to word of mouth, along with coverage from local media including CHS.
Despite five years of tinkering, the menu’s heart hasn’t moved. “Katsu is always going to be the heart of Kobuta & Ookami,” Phuksopha said.

A few appetizers and entrées have been added along the way, but the team has kept things deliberately tight. A smaller menu means faster service and more consistent training, essential in the tiny Capitol Hill dining room and kitchen. Many of the dishes from the original menu remain among the most popular today.
The biggest surprise of running a katsu-focused restaurant? “Probably how much people really love katsu!”

The dish looks simple, Phuksopha said, but the pork, breading, oil, temperature, texture and timing all matter, and customers notice. Keeping something that simple consistent every day takes constant work on staffing, training and equipment.
“Five years later, we’re still learning.”
As for why customers keep coming back, Phuksopha points to comfort, consistency and price. “It’s crispy, hot, satisfying and simple. When it’s done well, you crave it,” they said.
Phuksopha wants Kobuta & Ookami to be an everyday spot rather than a special-occasion splurge, something that has gotten harder with inflation, tariffs and rising ingredient costs.
The neighborhood around the restaurant has shifted, too. Phuksopha and crew have watched businesses open and close and new residents move in.
Kobuta & Ookami is part of a cluster of Capitol Hill food and drink in this block of 15th Ave E with Bakery Nouveau, Teriyaki Madness , and Aviv Hummus Bar nearby.

Lunch has gotten quieter as work patterns have changed, pushing the team to think more creatively about giving people reasons to stop by on weekdays. They also cited more visible homelessness and concerns about safety and property crime in their of Capitol Hill, saying they hope those issues continue to get attention so staff, customers and neighbors feel safe.

Then there are costs. Food, labor, insurance, utilities, “Inflation has affected almost everything,” they said. “Restaurants already operate on pretty small margins, so trying to keep prices reasonable while maintaining quality and taking care of our staff gets harder every year.”
There’s more competition, too, but Phuksopha say they’d rather focus on their own food and service.
“Capitol Hill is where Kobuta & Ookami started, so that location will always be really special to us.”
The team came to katsu from a Thai food background, but their love of Japanese food, animation and culture goes back to childhood. Travel deepened that appreciation, and changed how they eat.
“Before, we were mostly just eating and thinking, ‘This is so good.’ Now our restaurant brains never completely turn off,” they said. Breading, oil, plates, signs, lighting, they notice all of it.

Sake and Sapporo can be an important part of the experience, and Phuksopha said they want to lean into the drinks side even more. The sake list rotates as the team tastes new bottles, with an emphasis on keeping things approachable.
“You shouldn’t have to know everything about sake to order a glass and enjoy it,” they said. “Obviously we can’t bring Japan to Seattle, but we can bring a little bit of that feeling here.”

The third Kobuta & Ookami is planned for Mountlake Terrace in 2027. Phuksopha said they chose the location partly because customers farther north kept telling them they wanted to visit without fighting traffic into Seattle or Redmond.

The bigger space will let the team lean further into the Japanese yokocho, or alley, feel, with more sake, Japanese-style drinks and highballs, and a few new dishes, while keeping tonkatsu at the center.
Over the next five years, Phuksopha wants each location to have its own personality while still feeling like Kobuta & Ookami. And down the line, maybe something entirely new.
“We have a lot of ideas, but nothing we’re ready to announce yet.”
Kobuta & Ookami is located at121 15th Ave E. Learn more at kobutaandookami.com .

articles.title: ICE Still Outsmarting Washington’s Driver Data Protections
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: Washington state officials have made it harder for immigration agents to access driving records during deportation raids, but keep getting played by Trump’s deportation goons.

That’s according to a new report from the University of Washington Center for Human Rights (UWCHR). The report released Tuesday claims that current Department of Licensing practices still likely violate state laws protecting Washington state drivers from the disclosure of names, addresses, and license plate information for civil immigration enforcement.
Cruising around neighborhoods, malls, and other public spaces in Washington, ICE is able to look up driver information from state databases, despite laws prohibiting them from doing so.

“Most of these cases happen when people were driving, or close to their vehicles, or inside their vehicles,” said Guillermo Rivera, with Eastside For All, at a presentation of the report in a corner of a UW library. “We need accountability, and we need leadership now, not months from now.”
It’s not supposed to be like that in so-called “sanctuary states” like Washington.

The 2019 Keep Washington Working Act bars “nonpublicly available personal information” from local governments to federal immigration authorities “in a noncriminal matter, except as required by state or federal law.” But the enforcement of the law is patchy, and the state hasn’t caught up with changing tactics by immigration agencies, the report found.

Titled “ Stopping the DMV-to-DHS Data Pipeline ,” the report compares vehicle and driver data sharing between state and federal immigration across Washington, Maryland, Minnesota, and New York. The report identifies four pathways which driver data reaches immigration agents: directly through state databases, an interstate messaging system called Nlets, local law enforcement, and private data brokers.

The report looked at states with so-called “sanctuary” laws that profess to protect drivers’ privacy from federal immigration agents. (California, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Virginia, and Oregon didn’t share their data.)

Despite significant actions inconveniencing ICE, Washington still lets Customs and Border Protection (Border Patrol agents and Customs officers) access to car owner names and addresses through the interstate messaging system called Nlets.

In one example cited by the report, the interstate messaging platform Nlets was accessed by CBP to lead to an ICE arrest with no CBP agents present, suggesting ICE logged in with a CBP username, or asked for a lookup.
Immigration agencies blocked by Washington are logging in “just like you might share your Netflix password with a family member,” said UWCHR Director Angelina Godoy.

The news comes amid conflicting reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in Washington state, but a clear uptick in ICE enforcement nationwide ahead of the midterm elections . ICEwatch tracker IceOut.org published evidence Monday based on local arrest reports that some of the ICE enforcement in Washington has been shifted to California.
Gov. Bob Ferguson has attempted to disrupt the DOL to DHS data pipeline, according to the report. To understand what he’s been up to, here’s a refresher on immigration agency jargon:

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) goes after immigrants internally using Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) agents to arrest. Those agents used to operate separately from ICE’s detective wing, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). Those real cops used to focus squarely on human trafficking and other transnational crime. Customs and Border Protection, which is supposed to guard the border, has also been reassigned under Trump, sending agents to back up ERO.

Sound complicated? Well, if the state simply required a warrant from immigration agencies to use its data, it wouldn’t be. According to the report, that’s what New York State did, and it’s closed a lot of loopholes.

Washington’s approach is piecemeal. Under Ferguson, the state is trying to balance the role of federal agencies going after criminals and the White House hijacking criminal investigators to carry out mass deportations. It’s a game of whack-a-mole that Washington has accepted for the remainder of Trump’s term.
For example, according to Ferguson, CBP still needs access to Nlets to combat human trafficking and firearm access.

“ My team has worked to limit Customs and Border Protection access for immigration enforcement, while maintaining access necessary to protect public safety, such as human trafficking investigations that require real-time access to data to protect vulnerable Washingtonians,” Ferguson’s statement read. “Looking ahead to the next two years, this will be an ongoing process for us to adapt to what federal government does next to work around what we do to protect our data .”

Ferguson’s office told The Stranger how many queries it has blocked from immigration agents (174,349 from November 2025 to October 2026), but not how many were granted. The report says 3,696,147 data searches for driver and vehicle information have happened—though the numbers are not completely comparable because they are over a broader time frame (January 2025 to May 2026).

The UW report questions why that game should be played. It points out that victims of various immigration authority data theft have apparently never been notified of their data being given away illegally. A spokesperson for the governor declined to name an example of a notification, and did not contract the report’s finding.

The deportation machine, long focused on targeting immigrants who posed safety threats, is ramping up to unprecedented levels of not just xenophobia but illegality. Racial profiling, rubber stamped by the Supreme Court, is now the norm. Apprehending legal immigrants, and lying to courts to cover up illegal arrests, are shockingly common. And HSI, which used to quietly work with local police to solve international crimes, has been demoted from detective to beat cop.
Responses to these problems have been stronger in other states. Not only is New York state demanding warrants, it’s also historically funded immigrant legal defense at higher levels.

Many immigrants across Washington were already afraid to get in their cars, take their kids to the park, or even go grocery shopping in this so-called sanctuary state. As I’ve reported before , even immigrants who have beaten ICE in court travel nervously, packing an absurd number of documents with them as a kind of safety blanket against anticipated arrests and harassment.

Immigrants in Washington state keep getting arrested, with the assistance of data produced by their own tax dollars, in a regressive tax state where they contribute disproportionately to their income. Their data is casually released by politicians who are supposed to represent their interests (yes, non-voters are constituents), and answer to the family members and neighbors who voted them in. The report is a reminder that the laws voters supported to protect immigrants’ civil rights aren’t fully being enforced.

articles.title: Pop Loser: Pretty Woman’d at the Curiosity Shop
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! This week, Kelly Clarkson feuded with a Brooklyn curiosity shop over an animatronic bird, Britney Spears dropped an unreleased song from Britney , and Mariah Carey saw The Last Supper . I’ll share my go-to album for the fall season. Plus, Halloween came early—the trailer dropped for the new documentary about the Shaggs.

This week in Strangerland, I attended the new Styled by the Streets exhibit at MOPOP which features two of Lil Kim’s iconic wigs (gasp!). Dave Segal wrote about some new music you shouldn’t miss . Eva Walker shared the goth magic of classic blues in her Dear Hendrix column. Plus, Jullianne Bell and I unleashed the second installment of our Scarecrow Psychotronic Movie challenge picks, offering a fucked-up movie recommendation for every day of October. Stay tuned for week three, dropping this Thursday.

Kelly Clarkson got Pretty Woman’d at a curiosity shop. It’s a tale as old as time: famous singer/talk show host drives “all the way” to Brooklyn with the hopes of purchasing a $15,000 animatronic bird, but is “looked at” by the store clerk as if she can’t afford it. This is what happened to Clarkson on Saturday, and she took to X/Twitter to expose Art of Play, a boutique toy shop slinging a “unique collection of home goods, puzzles, games, toys and books.” The shop swiftly responded, explaining that “Molly,” the “one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton,” is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. Clarkson fired back with another lengthy post leveled at the shop owner, “You’re not only rude, you’re also a liar.”

Notably, “Molly” was created by Seattle-based automata builder Bliss Kolb , who offers a menagerie of wooden crank-operated birds and insects made to order on his website. Perhaps Clarkson should reach out directly.

Last Friday, Britney Spears released a never-before-heard 2001 song co-written with then-boyfriend Justin Timberlake . The unfinished track, titled “ She’ll Never Be Me ,” features background vocals by Timberlake and is being released in honor of the 25th anniversary of her third album, Britney.

The trailer for the new documentary about the Shaggs dropped. Directed by Ken Kwapis—whose filmography includes episodes of Freaks and Geeks and The Office — We Are the Shaggs shares insights from two of the Wiggins sisters as they reflect on the time their father forced them to start a band. Their 1969 album, Philosophy of the World, would later become a favorite of Kurt Cobain and Frank Zappa.

Olivia Rodrigo announced (via a photo from a recent video shoot) that her new song “Expectations,” featuring Chappell Roan, will be out this Thursday . As singer-songwriter Eliza McLamb commented, “God featuring Jesus release the Bible.”

Speaking of Olivia Rodrigo, she owns Meg White’s Elephant dress. Speaking to the Hollywood Reporter , Rodrigo revealed that she spent an “exorbitant amount of money” on the white Gunne Sax dress worn by White Stripes drummer Meg White on the cover of Elephant. What exactly is “exorbitant”? Well, according to Julian’s Auctions , the dress sold for $25,600. Rodrigo also shared that she had planned to wear the dress at the inaugural Daisy Chain Fields Music Festival, but backed out because it was “too fucking hot.” Adding, “Maybe if I do Daisy Chain in the winter, I can wear it.”
Now, take a deep breath and enjoy… Mariah Carey viewing Leonardo da Vinci’s The Last Supper .

articles.title: Five Films to See at the Seattle Trans Underground Film Festival
articles.author: Chase Hutchinson
paras: The Seattle Trans Underground Film Festival (STUFF) returns this week, proving that independent and trans cinema is not only alive, but thriving. With a variety of features and shorts, it’s the local film festival to attend this week.
The fest runs October 15 through the 18 at the Northwest Film Forum ( now open all week long! ). Here are five highlights you definitely don’t want to miss.

Directed by May Matchim, the opening night feature is a queer ecology documentary about the diversity of sexuality and gender in what Matchim calls “the fantastically queer” place that is nature. Both self-reflexive and sincere, Amphibian is a film that doesn’t fall into easy boxes. It flags early on that it’s not going to use the framing of certain things being “natural” to make queerness more palatable. Instead, Amphibian evolves in scope and ambition, gently confronting some of its own preconceived notions and narratives to create a portrait of all the complex, layered beauty to be found in existence. Though largely relying on a variety of talking head interviews, Amphibian also taps into something personal as we hear Matchim reflect on her own journey to accepting her transness, culminating in a poignant reflection that ties it all together perfectly.
Showing Thursday, October 15 at 6:30 p.m.

Next is a film that bravely asks what if you took Bertrand Bonello’s Nocturama, shot it like a mockumentary, kept the terrorism, added some satanism, and centered two of the most chaotic (complimentary) people you’ll ever meet? Gren Bee’s Trans Panic! follows Christian trans hyperpop musician Sara ‘T-Girl Nixon’ Jordan (Mia Sabine) who links up with the insecure intersex incel filmmaker Cody ‘Yung AJ’ Jones (Gren Bee) in order to carry out a terrorist attack to launch a music career and possibly also catch the attention of JD Vance like a reverse John Hinckley Jr. What could possibly go wrong? As it turns out, quite a lot. The pseudo-hangout movie is off-kilter even before it descends into complete chaos. But for those who can get on its wavelength, Trans Panic! ‘s cheeky provocations and freewheeling approach pay off and build to a bloody finale that gets its pound of flesh and then some.

Raef Van Putten’s Jucks is an experimental sci-fi silent film with the most striking visuals of the festival. Shot entirely in black-and-white, it takes us far into the future—2064 AD, to be precise—with a troubled protagonist known as Jules as they navigate a dystopian hellscape (Denver City) in search of gold. This description still only barely scratches the surface of what’s in store for you as this film. Without any spoken words, it boasts an entrancing, droning score that doubles as an all-consuming radio frequency in the film, drowning everything else out. For those who can surrender themselves to this oddity, they’ll find something truly spellbinding.
Showing Saturday, October 17 at 4:30 p.m.

Louise Weard’s Castration Movie Chapter iii.ii Junior Ghosts—Premorphic Drift; a fragmentary passage is the feel-bad movie of the festival. For those not familiar with Weard’s filmography, this is one of several Castration Movies and lifts its characters from a prior entry. However, no prior Castration knowledge is required, as this one tells a self-contained story. And it’s Weard’s best entry yet. Following Izzy (played by Avalon Fast) as she desperately tries to stop her partner, Tiffany (Henri Gillespi), from transitioning, the film is both funnier and more painful than it sounds. Weard brings plenty of satirical bite to key scenes before bringing down the emotional hammer in the intimate moments between the couple. While you’ll feel a pit in your stomach all the way until the final lines, you’ll be hard-pressed to find a more potent character study at the festival this year.

Last but definitely not least is Deathbed (no, not 1977’s Death Bed: The Bed That Eats ). Rather, this film is a scrappy, bite-sized, lo-fi local gem, about a haunting that disrupts a friend group. It’s filmed across Seattle (including in the Northwest Film Forum itself!). This already makes it worth seeing for that alone, but it’s also got some other tricks up its sleeves. Without giving anything away, there are some sinister scenes where the picture begins to distort and warp, drawing you in before snapping back to “normal.” Even when it’s a little rough around the edges, this is a feature, not a bug, with the crackling and distorting audio getting under your skin. It builds to visuals of ghosts taking shape out of static that may just haunt you as well.
Showing Sunday, October 18 at 7:30 p.m. as part of the WE LIVE shorts program
Still haven’t gotten your tickets? You can fix that by getting individual tickets here or a full pass here .
