articles.title: 'The Ave for All' Transforms U District's Main Thoroughfare
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seeing a street festival take over University Way NE through the heart of the U District is a common sight throughout most of the year. But this past Saturday, the attraction wasn't food vendors or craftspeople – it was the street itself. Visitors to one of the city's most beloved shopping districts were treated to a fully pedestrianized street as part of " The Ave for All ", which continues this upcoming Saturday, October 17 for a second weekend.

An idea advanced by the placemaking group U District Advocates, The Ave for All gives pedestrians breathing room to enjoy a leisurely Saturday without being crammed onto University Way's narrow sidewalks. Tables and chairs turned the periphery of the street into a patio that wasn't tied to any specific businesses, prompting more folks to stick around and linger... but also grab a bite nearby.

Games, including a large chess board, provided activation and a pair of buskers livened the mood. It didn't hurt that storm clouds, spitting rain in the early afternoon, cleared away and left a beautiful autumn day.
For event organizer L. Harrison Jerome, the Ave for All is a glimpse of how a neighborhood like the University District can better use one of its biggest stretches of real estate – the street.

"In this neighborhood, you see how thin the sidewalks are. Now people actually have the ability to move out into the space, and they're actually filling it," Jerome told The Urbanist. "They're doing chalk art, they're hanging out with each other, they're playing games, they're having off street dining. It's really, really nice weather today, and people are just enjoying the street in a different way than they had before."

As a broader city, Seattle is taking small steps toward creating more pedestrian-oriented spaces out of underutilized stretches of roadway, with the Seattle Department of Transportation's People Streets and Public Spaces program at the forefront of that work. Potential public plazas are being eyed in the Admiral District, Delridge, and on Upper Queen Anne, projects that will ultimately be demonstrations of the idea of creating a pedestrian plaza at the heart of every neighborhood.
But The Ave for All is presenting a bolder vision of how a street at the heart of a business district can truly transform.

U District Advocates has pointed out that they are not the first group to dream of a fully pedestrian-oriented Ave, with storied Seattle architect Victor Steinbrueck putting the idea forward in 1955. The idea got closest to becoming a reality in the early 1970s, with the University District Development Council established specifically to advance the idea.

"The plan basically calls for a pedestrian mall on University Way NE to run from NE 47th to NE 42nd streets," a February 1972 story in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer noted. At that time, outgoing UDDC Executive Vice President David Rowlands touted the proposal for a U District pedestrian mall as creating "what Ghirardelli Square is to San Francisco, what the French Quarter is to New Orleans and what George-town is to Washington, D.C."

The year before in 1971, UDDC surveyed participants at the U District Street Fair finding 90% general support for the idea of a pedestrian mall ( sound familiar? ). But the proposal fell apart when property owners on the Ave were required to provide their stamp of approval. An alternative proposal put forward by neighborhood real estate broker Don Kennedy included a pedestrian plaza in front of what is now the UW tower connected to a "tremendous" parking garage with shops on top. That idea never came to fruition either.

Everything old is new again. Earlier this summer, the U District Advocates had a false start after the City of Seattle declined to approve an initial request to open up the Ave in late May and early June , with a number of nearby business owners opposing the plan.

As the Seattle Times reported at the time, the push back was orchestrated by Lois Ko and Emily Scully, owners of Sweet Alchemy and Shultzy’s Bar & Grill respectively. But after other business owners in the neighborhood found they'd been added to a list of opponents of the event without their knowledge, a cloud of animus and uncertainty grew up around the entire project that threatened to sour the spirit of The Ave for All.

While that's not exactly ancient history at this point, it did seem to be put in the rearview mirror this weekend. For the autumn re-do, U District Advocates was asked to jump through a few more hoops to show they'd conducted community outreach, a bar they were ultimately able to clear.

"One thing I learned from that it's sort of difficult for community groups to do things like this," Jerome said. "We know that there's a huge amount of support for reprioritizing a ton of our streets back toward people rather than cars, but it's really difficult for people to voice those wants."

What the future holds for The Ave is impossible to know. But based on the turnout this past weekend, there's clear demand for something to draw people out into the street, even without a food festival.

"We'd love to do this event again," Jerome said. "We want to work with the City and the businesses and the local community, the residents, the students, get everybody in the conversation to actually talk about what a city pilot of this could actually look like, where we do it day-to-day or on weekends, sometime in the spring or the summer."
U District residents and visitors will have one more chance to visit The Ave for All this Saturday from 11am to 8pm.

articles.title: Tacoma Pushes to Reimagine Crash-Prone Portland Avenue
articles.author: Carolyn Bick
paras: Anthony E. Jackson moved from Seattle to a home in the mixed-income Salishan development in Tacoma 13 years ago. Since then, the retired 63-year-old Army veteran has been actively involved in life in the Tacoma Housing Authority development, and serves on the neighborhood’s homeowners association board.
In that time, Jackson has become intimately familiar with the conditions along Portland Avenue, one of the city’s most dangerous roads.

“You got the traffic lights there. I think that's a great thing they put in [ … ] but other than that, you just got to pay attention to what you're doing. [ … ] When two o'clock comes, the flow of traffic picks up. Another thing is, you got big communities on both sides of Portland Avenue, and it's continued to grow,” Jackson said. “That's going to cause a lot of cars utilizing Portland Avenue to get to their homes or go to work. It's still kind of hectic.”

Jackson isn’t alone in his observations. The road’s dangerous conditions have been a focal point for the area’s overlapping communities for some time. In addition to running through Puyallup Tribe land, the road stretches through Tacoma’s Eastside, a community still bearing the brunt of racist urban planning practices, including redlining and underinvestment in infrastructure. In its Transportation Improvement Plan, the City also named Portland Avenue as one of its highest crash-risk corridors.

These physical and historic social conditions are why the City of Tacoma, in close collaboration with the Puyallup Tribe, has been pursuing an ongoing overhaul of the road as part of the City’s Vision Zero initiative , meant to eliminate traffic fatalities and reduce traffic-related injuries by 2035.

Additionally, if voters pass a ballot measure boosting Pierce Transit funding in November, the road may get another upgrade that could go a long way towards improving road safety: a new, longer bus route that would provide direct north-to-south access along Portland Avenue.

The goal is to create a Portland Avenue that is significantly safer, supports better living conditions, and opens up transit options for all, especially for historically underserved communities who have long had to go the extra mile — proverbial or otherwise — to access equal living and working opportunities in Tacoma.

In its 2015 Safety Plan , the Puyallup Tribe was the first to identify severe safety issues along the portion of Portland Avenue that runs straight through Tribal land. The Tribe’s subsequent 2016 safety audit comprehensively reviewed the road’s poor, dangerous conditions.

“East Portland Avenue is the primary arterial to reach essential services which include Tribal Government, Housing, Police, Gaming, and Health,” the 2015 plan reads. “This route has a high posted speed limit and high pedestrian counts. There are few places to cross the street and the level of service during rush hour is routinely failing.”

Robert Barandon, the Tribe’s director of planning and land use, said in an email that the Tribe incorporated Portland Avenue into the plan and audit, because it “is a very important corridor for the Tribe as it is a primary arterial and adjacent to many Tribal facilities, businesses, and essential services.”
In 2020, the city released its Vision Zero plan, which intentionally incorporated Tribe-identified safety issues that needed to be rectified, including the conditions of Portland Avenue.

Laura Svancarek, who is executive director of Tacoma On The Go, said that the traffic on the road is “very high-speed, high-traffic,” and that it’s “very unpleasant to walk on the sidewalks along it, but particularly unpleasant and unsafe feeling to cross Portland Avenue because it is so high-speed and high-traffic.”
The wideness of the road is likely linked to rampant speeding — a well-documented relationship many safe streets advocates and practitioners have noted .

“It's a very wide roadway as well. Generally speaking, it’s a real thoroughfare of a road in that way, because when you look at it in the context of the Eastside, it starts to become even more of a severe issue,” Svancarek continued.
In addition to several Tribal buildings and parks along the road, the Pacific Cultural Center was located in a building on Portland Avenue for several years.

“[On] the Eastside of Tacoma, you see a lot more communities of color, folks from the Tribe, folks who are low-income, and so it combines into this systemic issue,” Svancarek said. “You kind of get stuck on one side of Portland Avenue, and if you are not someone that's able to drive whenever you want to, it very much separates you from other resources and the rest of the city in what can feel like a more industrial area, especially as you get closer to the [Port of Tacoma].”

Even though he owns two cars, Jackson has seen how bad the sidewalks are. He said that he used to be unable to cross the road on foot to get to the different stores on the other side, including the grocery store.

“It was a nightmare, but I think they put some measurements in place like safer pedestrian crosswalks. [ … ] I've seen [the City] working on that — improving the sidewalk, the walking conditions, working on the stops, the traffic lights and stuff like that — because usually there are a lot of accidents,” he said. He noted that the City installed more obvious pedestrian crosswalks close to where he lives, and that “those things look really good. [ … ] They're putting that work effort in place.”

Svancarek also highlighted that national statistics show that Indigenous people suffer the highest rate of traffic-related deaths: “You see that repeat itself here in Tacoma and Pierce County, when you look at the type of roadways that intersect with Tribal land.”

The Puyallup Tribe’s 2015 Safety Plan states that between 2010 and 2013, the road within the boundaries of the Puyallup Indian Reservation saw a total of 154 reported crashes. Of those, five resulted in major injuries, and 65 resulted in minor injuries. Eighty-four resulted in property damage.

Most of the crashes happened during the daytime on dry roads. Tribal officials attributed a majority of crashes to a failure to yield, followed by driver inattention or distraction. More than 80% of the crashes happened at intersections or driveways.

In 2023, the City secured a $2.1 million grant from the Federal Highway Administration’s Transportation Alternatives Program to fund community engagement regarding Portland Avenue and the work to plan and design the road.

During this preliminary phase, City staff is identifying the best possible places for upgrades along the road. These upgrades include incorporating bicycle lanes and pedestrian access, as well as planting trees and vegetation.

If the City identifies design needs that extend beyond the public right-of-way, Chavez said, it will need to buy those rights from private entities. This will require the City to spend additional money, but “we are always highly intentional about when and where we take that step.”
Chavez also said that the hope is to bring forward the City-identified cross-sections for community feedback next year.

“We’re going to be asking the community to give us some perspective of what it is they would like for us to implement. It could be that at the end of this exercise, we may probably utilize a combination of cross-sections — in some areas we can do more, in some areas we can do less,” he said.
Over the summer, the City held two community feedback sessions, one as an in-person event, and another as a survey. The in-person event attracted 93 people, and 161 people returned surveys.

The total feedback the City received underscored the need for safety improvements, including traffic calming measures — the road is notorious for speeding — improved and maintained sidewalk infrastructure, more crosswalks, and repaved road surface. The City plans to hold additional listening sessions beginning in the first quarter of 2027.

“The theme throughout all of it really was safety,” said City Transportation Division Manager Jennifer Kammerzell, reflecting on the feedback. “Some people just weren't comfortable walking along the route. There definitely wasn't access for bicycles. [ … ] What we had heard is [that we need to work on] making it more walkable, having an alternative or some route for bicycle access. Slowing down traffic really was the biggest concern that we've heard previously, and then even in our current engagement as well.”
Barandon said that the Tribe would work with the City to weigh in on potential alternatives to proposed improvements.

“As it progresses beyond that and actual projects or improvements are programmed there is opportunity to partner and help the City to acquire funding,” he said. “Again, it’s early in the process, but we are hoping to get more information soon.”

Kammerzell also said that she meets with the Tribe on a monthly basis to work on transportation-related projects, including Portland Avenue. She said that the Tribe is looking towards diversifying and activating more of their commercial areas, particularly with their new casino, entertainment district, and administration building, as well as the new Portland Avenue station planned as part of Sound Transit’s Tacoma Dome Link Extension Project , which is slated to open in 2035.

“Even right now, their casino is expanding and they’re building a new parking garage,” she said. “I've been working with their development team on what their Portland Avenue improvement might look like, and how could that complement a future Portland Avenue Vision Zero corridor project.”

The City has also installed honorary Twulshootseed (the language of the Puyallup Tribe) street signs on the portion of Portland Avenue that runs through Tribal land, as part of a street naming partnership with the Puyallup Tribe. The Twulshootseed name for Portland Avenue is dukʷibəł (in English, “The Changer”), referring to the Lushootseed creation story , in which dukʷibəł moves through the land, changing creatures and plants into who they are today.

Chavez said that the Portland Avenue project will be “very expensive.” But where the funding comes from and ultimately how much the City will need will be determined by how final improvement and design plans shake out.

“We really don't have any of those elements in place yet, because we really don't know how we're going to be proceeding in terms of the design itself until we get the feedback from the community and landing on the potential cross-sections that we need to implement on this,” he explained. “It most likely will be built in phases. We cannot just secure funding for this long corridor. [ … ] When we get to the point of defining the potential phases, then we're going to start targeting as to what potential grant funding could be an avenue that could help us construct this corridor.”

Though the City’s roadwork is neither tied to nor dependent upon Pierce Transit’s ballot measure, if the measure goes through, Chavez said, it could create more opportunities to explore future roadwork.

The transit agency’s ballot measure, Proposition 1 , includes a new, longer, more frequent bus route along Portland Avenue, as well as upgrades to existing bus routes. These Portland Avenue-specific upgrades are part of a package of transit improvements Pierce Transit will be bringing to voters in November. That package is funded through a local sales tax increase of 0.3% — bringing the agency’s sales tax up from 0.6% to 0.9% — and would take effect April 1, 2027, if approved.
While Pierce Transit does operate two buses, the Route 41 and Route 54 , along Portland Avenue, neither serves the portion of the road stretching between E 32nd Street and E 38th Street.

Tacoma City Councilmember Kristina Walker, who serves on the Pierce Transit board, said that she “would call [the available buses] a lifeline service — there's not nothing, but it's certainly not convenient.”

articles.title: Relaunched Community Court Gets Paired With Punitive Repeat Offender System
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: The Seattle City Attorney’s Office (CAO) has announced two new programs affecting its handling of misdemeanor criminal cases in Seattle: a new community court called Connections Court and a new repeat offender system called the High-Priority Repeat Offenses (HiPRO) program. Both programs are being launched despite concerns expressed by the King County Department of Public Defense (DPD).

“Connection Court restores a key prosecution alternative with new accountability, and our HiPRO protocols seek firmer consequences for those who have taken advantage of Seattle's compassion,” Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans said in a press release.

Evans took office at the beginning of the year after delivering a rousing defeat to the former City Attorney, Republican Ann Davison. On the campaign trail, Evans promised to undo many of the harms of her predecessor, including beginning a new community court program to replace the one Davison had unilaterally shut down.
Less than ten months after taking office, Evans is delivering on that promise.

“Connection Court is a much-welcomed successor to its failed predecessors for importantly it centers on the participants and their needs but also accountability,” said Seattle Councilmember Bob Kettle, the chair of the public safety committee . “ I thank City Attorney Evans for furthering a more functional criminal justice system, which is crucial in creating a safer Seattle.”

Not everyone is as happy about Evans’ changes to this iteration of community court, the previous version of which was launched in 2020 by former City Attorney Pete Holmes. The biggest critic of the new programs is King County DPD.

Being the watchdog of CAO is nothing new for DPD, which spoke out against many of Davison’s policies. In addition to objecting to Davison’s ending of the former community court program, DPD opposed Davison’s High Utilizers Initiative and her Stay Out of Drug Area (SODA) and Stay Out of Areas of Prostitution (SOAP) exclusion orders . The department also drew attention to Davison’s enforcement of Seattle’s 2023 drug ordinance, which had a disproportionate impact on Black people based on City data and wasn’t resulting in the promised diversion.

Some hoped that with Evans in office, there would be a new ability of CAO and DPD to cooperate. But DPD told The Urbanist that Evans’ office didn’t inform them about the new HiPRO program until Monday, October 5, the day the new community court opened. As of Thursday afternoon, DPD hadn’t received any written protocols on the new system.

“I would say that we are disappointed by the HiPRO initiative and by the restrictions on who's eligible for Connection Court,” DPD’s Special Counsel for Criminal Policy and Practice Katie Hurley told The Urbanist .

On the criminal side, CAO only handles lower-level cases – misdemeanors and gross misdemeanors – while felonies are handled by the King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office (KCPAO). In practice, this distinction means that many of the referrals CAO receives from the Seattle Police Department (SPD) involve crimes of poverty, oftentimes with a nexus of behavioral health conditions, although the office also handles some domestic violence and driving-under-the-influence cases.
Going forward, people who have been charged with a low-level, nonviolent offense without a pattern of repeated criminal misconduct may be sent through Evans’ new Connection Court.

“How I sum up Connection Court, it’s an opportunity to provide meaningful services to participants in the program so they get what they need to be okay, and then after 90 days, their case gets dismissed,” Evans told The Urbanist . “That is the summary of it, and I want it also really clear that we are still very robust in pre-file and post-file diversion, and this is just an additional layer.”

The new court program is being run at no additional cost to the City, providing an assessment with a court counselor to participants to determine which services would be the most appropriate for their individual needs. Evans talked about a menu of different services that includes medication-assisted substance use disorder treatment, help applying for health insurance, prescription delivery, mental health treatment, food, and ORCA cards. Participants will also have the opportunity to apply for jobs as downtown ambassadors with the Metropolitan Improvement District.

Evans is hoping to expand the program in the future, potentially hosting it at a local library and providing pet fostering for people who want to go into substance use treatment. And she has been in conversation with the Mayor’s Office about the possibility of setting aside a certain number of tiny homes or other shelter spots for participants in the program.

“I am very optimistic and hopeful that as we continue to grow and what we're able to provide for Connection Court, that the opportunity to have beds set aside for folks going through Connection Court is not only possible, but an absolute need for folks that are participating in the program,” Evans said.
Connection Court has a few key differences from its predecessor. These differences, which Kettle applauded, are points of contention between Evans’ office and DPD.

In the past, participants in community court would have their cases dismissed upon completion of the program, a policy supported by DPD. However, Evans has insisted on a 90-day jurisdiction period, regardless of how long the program engagements take, during which participants will need to avoid arrest in order to successfully complete the program. Participants also have to prove they’ve engaged with at least two different services.
Failure to meet either of these requirements and they could be sent back to mainstream court for criminal prosecution.

“We have to have a longer period to make sure we're actually engaging with participants,” Evans said. “I want to make sure that this is something that's going to be successful, and I know from us doing these cases, that's not in one day.”
DPD, on the other hand, believes cases should be dismissed when a participant successfully completes their engagement.

DPD also opposes stricter eligibility rules to the program. Evans has instituted eligibility restrictions for Connections Court based on prior criminal history, another change from the former community court. And Hurley said people will also be excluded if they are being held in custody for another offense, possibly because they are unable to afford their bail.

“We're really alarmed at that exclusion as well, as it denies the Connection Court pathway for people because they're not able to afford bail, and that's related to a case, a charge, where they're presumed innocent,” Hurley said.
Finally, people who are routed to the new HiPRO initiative won’t be eligible for Connection Court.

“These restrictions exclude the very people for whom a Connection Court is really most needed: those people struggling with homelessness, with behavioral health, who need support and help addressing underlying issues, rather than an aggravated jail sentence,” Hurley said.

The new HiPRO program will apply to cases where people who have been charged by the CAO either three times in three months or six times in six months. In addition, cases can be routed into the program immediately if a person has shoplifted in a store where they have previously been trespassed or if they’re being charged for a car prowl case (breaking into a vehicle) and have a conviction of felony theft, car theft, or robbery in the last year.
People with a case flagged for the HiPRO program will be ineligible for either diversion or Connection Court, and attorneys will ask for longer sentences for these cases.

“We're making sure we're giving folks opportunities for those services and treatment,” Evans said. “You know, one time, two times, and then I think it is important to have some accountability, you know, a third time. Otherwise, there is no incentive to [say], okay, maybe I should think about this and engage in some way.”
Hurley had a different view on the program, saying it will exacerbate current issues at the Seattle Municipal Court.

“They're going to be asking for aggravated jail sentences for low-level property offenses,” Hurley said. “Almost all of those folks are experiencing homelessness and/or behavioral health disorders, and it's going to be very expensive for the City. If judges were to impose these jail sentences, it's going to make it less likely that we'll be able to resolve cases and will likely result in more trials as we vindicate our clients' rights, and will make it so that we don't actually address the underlying needs people have. You're going to pay a lot of money for a system to try to punish folks whose basic needs aren't being met.”

According to the press release about the program, “this approach lets prosecutors dynamically target patterns of individual behavior, rather than relying on a static list of names.” The reference to a list is a clear recall to Davison’s High Utilizers Initiative , which was in fact a list of frequent offenders with more than 12 misdemeanor referrals in five years. An investigation by PubliCola in 2022 showed that most of the people on this list were unhoused and many were suffering from major behavioral conditions, with almost half ordered to undergo a competency evaluation.
Evans said anyone with a major behavioral condition should be going through the mental health court and doesn’t think her program will have the same issues as the High Utilizers Initiative.
Hurley said that in some ways, the new HiPRO program is more expansive than Davison’s High Utilizers program due to its inclusion of shoplifting and car prowling.

“I was exceedingly surprised to see a theft related to someone who previously received a trespass notice be considered a HiPRO individual,” Hurley said. “That is a low-level behavior involving a nonviolent property offense, which almost always has no actual loss to the store.”
The CAO will be adding the ability to track the HiPRO cases to its data management system , although it is not clear when this new capability will be operational.
Evans emphasized that CAO attorneys will have complete discretion around decisions about eligibility for Connection Court and which cases to include in the HiPRO program.
But Hurley said it’s important to design systems with policies that make sense for the majority of cases coming through that system.

“It's hard for me to imagine in my mind a case that would not be appropriate for Connection Court where a person is charged with a low-level shoplift involving a business, including a trespass,” Hurley said. “And if you're going to rely on individual prosecutors, line prosecutors, to make decisions, it's going to invite bias. It's going to invite unequal decision making, and it's going to result in far more people being excluded from these pathways than we saw under the previous iteration of Connection Court.”

articles.title: Duplicative services and commuter route truncation, again
articles.author: Sherwin Lee
paras: We’re about a month into the Fall shakeup, where a substantial number of service changes were implemented to improve connections to Link. This is a recurring playbook that Metro has used ever since light rail service began: identify duplicative services and restructure existing bus routes to connect to Link stations rather than running all the way into downtown Seattle.

When Northgate Link opened, Sound Transit truncated many of its 510 series routes to connect at Link instead. After Lynnwood Link, all of Community Transit’s direct services to downtown Seattle were restructured . And with the August changes , both Metro and Sound Transit no longer offer any one-seat rides from Bellevue or Issaquah to Seattle, save for the 2 Line.

Critics of this approach generally lament the loss of the one-seat ride, that trip times generally increase when factoring in wait times, and that Link is not necessarily faster point-to-point than express routes. The Sound Transit subreddit and other various community forums feature countless examples of riders testifying to that end. There is even now a “Restore 554” petition circulating among Issaquah residents, urging the restoration of a direct Issaquah-Seattle route.

The planning justifications for this type of restructuring are quite straightforward: Link provides a frequent high-capacity serve to major regional centers; instead of running costly peak-directional bus service, reinvest the hours into boosting local connecting service. This implementation aligns with Jarrett Walker’s “frequency is freedom” mantra and is generally a position this blog has supported.

In practice, however, real-world conditions can muddy the picture. Take, for example, the 554’s successor: the 556, which now provides frequent all-day service between Issaquah and Bellevue. Those previously using the 554 (or the 550 local stops along Bellevue Way) to get to Seattle must now connect at South Bellevue Station for the same trip.

These transfer conditions can greatly deteriorate due to local northbound congestion on Bellevue Way just in the short span between the I-90 off-ramp and the station bus stops. Riders agonizingly wait for traffic to crawl up Bellevue Way only to see Seattle-bound trains glide past over their heads. Even in the southbound direction, buses have to yield to northbound traffic in order to turn into the station bays, which adds travel time variability.
The physical infrastructure in between the connecting services is important too. Jarrett Walker touches on this point in one of his foundational articles on transferring:

… the unpleasantness of the connection experience depends on many details of how the connection works. If two buses or trains arrive on opposite sides of a platform, facing one another five meters apart, with their doors open at the same time, walking out of one and into the other is a pretty low level of inconvenience for most passengers. If the connection involves getting off a bus, crossing a busy street, and waiting for another bus not knowing when it will arrive, the inconvenience is much greater.

As it were, the connecting infrastructure at South Bellevue and Mercer Island stations is less than ideal. Both settings require a moderate walk (across a signalized intersection in the latter case, largely thanks to Mercer Island’s opposition to an 80th Ave transfer point) and ascending or descending to the train platform. This can add a lot of variability, particularly for those with limited mobility, on top of the wait for the connecting service.

Negative feedback is often amplified over positive feedback, as human beings are far more likely to complain about things that hurt them rather than praise the things that help them. But in many ways, what is often seen as a degradation in one part of the network typically means an improvement in another part.

554 riders, for example, might glowingly reminisce about the quick travel times across I-90, but forget about the frequent outbound reliability issues inflicted by 2nd Avenue congestion (as I so often personally experienced). And although not quite a zero sum game, the changes have meant a substantially better commute for Issaquah-Bellevue riders, among other parts of the system.

Big restructures in the regional network will invariably result in system-wide tradeoffs, but that doesn’t mean agencies’ hands are tied. Barring a miraculous way of sending buses congestion-free right up (or down) to the Link platforms, transfer penalties can be offset by improving frequency and reliability across all segments.

Making the 556 a frequent all-day route that connects to frequent 2 Line service is certainly an excellent start, but continued work on reliability improvements are always in order. This might mean more attentive maintenance to ensure fewer breakdowns of Link trains. Or it could mean stronger partnerships with WSDOT and local jurisdictions to give signal or lane priority to buses.

Whatever the solution, transit agencies cannot go it alone here. Route 8’s dramatic reliability leaps were only possible by some repainting (and other minor infrastructural improvements) from SDOT. In the same way, local jurisdictions owe it to the taxpaying public to squeeze out the full return on our massive regional investment in transit. Helping create reliable well-connected services is a small, but important step to get there.

articles.title: Ballard Link Community Forum on October 19
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Seattle City Councilmember (District 6) and Sound Transit Boardmember Dan Strauss is hosting a community form discussing the Ballard Link Extension alongside several other elected officials and Sound Transit representatives. The forum will be held in the Osberg Great Hall at the National Nordic Museum on Monday, October 19, from 6-8pm .

In a newsletter emailed to constituents last week, Dan Strauss announced the event while highlighting his efforts to get Sound Transit to commit to building the full Ballard Link Extension to Market Street. These included requiring Sound Transit staff to determine when the agency would be able to complete the Ballard Link Extension under current conditions, and looking for ways to reduce project costs in order to open the extension sooner. Currently, the agency expects to open the SODO to Seattle Center portion of the Ballard Link Extension in 2042.

In July, Sound Transit fulfilled Strauss’ first requirement with the announcement the rest of the project could be delayed to 2060 unless significant cost savings are found. When voters passed ST3 in 2016, the entire Ballard Link Extension was expected to open in 2035. In 2021, this schedule slipped to 2037 or 2039 as Sound Transit realized the cost to build a second Link-only tunnel under downtown and managing other complications would far exceed expectations . After calculating “bottom-up” cost estimates for the proposed design of the extension last year, the agency found the full project could cost nearly twice its previous estimate. Compounded with exploding cost estimates across ST3, the Sound Transit Board voted to defer construction of line past Seattle Center until costs were reduced or additional revenue were found.

Sound Transit says it may be able to open the full extension in 2042 if the agency can reduce the total estimated cost by $1 billion (or identify that much in new revenue), begin acquiring property by 2030, finish design by 2032, and lock in funding to start construction by 2033. Regardless, Ballard Link advocates remain dedicated to pushing Sound Transit to return to the originally promised date of opening in 2035.

At the community forum, Sound Transit is expected to share more about its proposed timeline for the Ballard Link Extension, the work agency staff have been doing to reduce costs, and its next steps for the project. There will also be a Q&A session.

Those interested in a seat should probably arrive early. The National Nordic Museum is located at the intersection of 28th Ave NW and NW Market Street, just under a mile west of the planned terminus of the Ballard Link Extension. Nearby bus stops are served by King County Metro Routes 17 and 44 .

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
